According to the Rome IV criteria, FD is primarily classified into two subtypes, epigastric pain syndrome (EPS) and postprandial distress syndrome (PDS). 1 FD is prevalent globally, affecting an estimated 6.8%–11% of the population worldwide, 2 and significantly impairs patients’ quality of life. The condition also imposes a substantial economic burden, encompassing both direct medical costs and indirect costs from work absenteeism and reduced productivity. 3 Despite its high prevalence, the management of FD remains a challenging clinical issue, largely owing to its complex and incompletely understood pathophysiological mechanisms.

The pathogenesis of FD involves a complex interplay of mechanisms, including acid exposure, gastric motility disorders (e.g., delayed gastric emptying and impaired accommodation), visceral hypersensitivity, central nervous system dysregulation, psychosocial factors, and changes in the gut microbiota. 4 Among these proposed mechanisms, acid exposure has long been implicated as a key contributor to symptom generation. Although FD patients do not necessarily exhibit increased gastric acid secretion, accumulating evidence indicates heightened sensitivity to normal or even low levels of acid within the proximal gastrointestinal tract. 5 Duodenal acid infusion has been shown to provoke more severe dyspeptic symptoms in FD patients compared to healthy controls (HCs). Furthermore, emerging evidence suggests that impaired duodenal mucosal integrity plays a pivotal role in this process, as it may allow acid and other luminal contents to penetrate the epithelium and sensitize underlying nerves. 6

This established role of gastric acid in symptom pathogenesis has positioned acid-lowering therapy—particularly proton pump inhibitors (PPIs)—as a cornerstone of the empirical management of FD. 7 , 8 However, the overall efficacy of PPIs remains modest and inconsistent across patient populations. Meta-analyses indicate a number needed to treat (NNT) of approximately 10–15, indicating that a significant proportion of patients experience insufficient symptom relief. 9 This limitation highlights the necessity of critically reevaluating the role of PPIs within current treatment frameworks. Furthermore, emerging research on novel acid-suppressive agents and previously underrecognized non-acid-related mechanisms of PPI action—such as anti-inflammatory or visceral modulatory effects—offers promising new directions for understanding and managing FD. 10 , 11

Therefore, this review aims to comprehensively evaluate the role and efficacy of conventional acid-lowering agents in FD, as well as to explore the newly identified mechanisms of acid suppression relevant to this condition and the therapeutic potential of emerging acid-lowering agents.

THE ROLE OF ACID EXPOSURE IN THE PATHOGENESIS OF FD The pathophysiology of FD is multifactorial and complex, with multiple distinct mechanisms frequently coexisting in individual patients, thereby establishing a self-sustaining cycle of symptom persistence. Although established pathogenic factors now extend beyond conventional motor dysfunction and visceral hypersensitivity to encompass immune activation, gut microbial dysregulation, and epithelial barrier impairment, 4 acid exposure remains a pivotal contributor to FD symptomatology.

Despite the fact that the majority of FD patients have normal gastric acid secretion, 12 emerging evidence indicates heightened sensitivity to gastric acid in the stomach of these individuals. For example, a study conducted by Oshima et al. 13 revealed that FD patients are more susceptible to symptom generation following gastric acid or water infusion when compared to HCs, and the severity of these symptoms is significantly greater in these FD patients. Interestingly, such hypersensitivity is not observed in patients with Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection. 14 This heightened acid sensitivity may be linked to the upregulation of acid-sensing molecules, including transient receptor potential vanilloid 1, glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor, and nerve growth factor, in the gastric mucosa of FD patients. 15

Apart from the stomach, accumulating evidence has identified the duodenum as a key site of acid-mediated pathology in FD. Increased duodenal acid exposure has been consistently observed in FD patients. 16 In addition, duodenal acid infusion induces abdominal discomfort, bloating, nausea, and epigastric burning in healthy individuals. 5 , 17 It also impairs gastric motility in FD patients, leading to disrupted gastric accommodation. 18 Several mechanisms are linked to abnormal duodenal acid exposure and heightened sensitivity in FD. Increased acid exposure can undermine the integrity of the duodenal mucosal barrier, as characterized by dilated intercellular spaces. 19 - 21 This breach enables luminal antigens—such as bile acids, dietary components, and microorganisms—to penetrate the subepithelial layer and trigger inflammatory responses. This, in turn, can activate mucosal immunity. The hallmark of such activation is the increased infiltration and degranulation of immune cells, particularly eosinophils and mast cells, in the duodenal mucosa. 22 - 25 Upon activation, these cells release various mediators (e.g., histamine, tryptases, cytokines) that can directly sensitize nearby visceral afferent nerves. This process lowers the pain perception threshold and contributes to visceral hypersensitivity. 26 Sensitized visceral afferent nerves may exacerbate duodenal inflammation, thereby reinforcing a self-perpetuating cycle of inflammatory responses and symptom generation. Supporting this hypothesis, researchers have found that the degree of impaired duodenal barrier integrity is correlated with the number of adjacent eosinophils and mast cells, 20 , 21 , 27 and PPI treatment can significantly restrain the infiltration of eosinophils, supporting a strong link between acid exposure and immune activation. Moreover, dysbiosis resulting from impaired duodenal barrier function and immune activity may play an important role in the pathogenesis, as alterations in microbiota abundance, predominantly in the duodenum, are correlated with the severity of symptoms, gastric emptying, and gut-brain axis interaction. 28 - 30

Furthermore, altered esophageal acid exposure has been demonstrated in a subset of FD patients. This is particularly relevant for the EPS subtype, where symptoms like epigastric burning are more frequently associated with pathological gastroesophageal acid reflux. 31 The link between esophageal acid and EPS symptoms can be conceptualized through two interconnected mechanisms: direct mucosal irritation from refluxate and acid-induced visceral hypersensitivity. Importantly, the increased acid exposure itself may not be a primary driver but rather a secondary phenomenon. It is hypothesized to stem from impaired gastric accommodation, a core motor dysfunction in FD. This impairment can promote acid reflux by triggering more frequent transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxations, 16 , 31 , 32 thereby linking gastric sensorimotor abnormalities to esophageal acid events and subsequent EPS symptoms. 33

Collectively, acid contributes to FD through heightened sensitivity in the stomach and esophagus. In the duodenum, its involvement is more complex, initiating a pathological cascade characterized by mucosal barrier disruption, low-grade inflammation, microbial dysbiosis, and neuronal sensitization.

THE EFFICACY OF ACID SUPPRESSION IN FD The management of FD remains empirical, given its heterogeneous nature and the lack of a universally effective targeted therapy. Current treatment guidelines recommend a step-wise approach that often begins with reassurance and dietary modification. 7 , 8 , 34 Pharmacological interventions are tailored to the predominant symptoms. Due to the common overlap between subtypes and the significant role of acid exposure in pathogenesis, PPIs have secured a cornerstone position in the empirical management of FD. 7 , 8 , 34 Other commonly used agents include histamine-2-receptor antagonists (H2RAs), prokinetics (e.g., domperidone, itopride), tricyclic antidepressants, or herbal medicine.

The efficacy of PPIs in FD is well-established, though modest. This has secured their position as a first-line treatment, despite the fact that not all patients respond. This conclusion is primarily supported by meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), which consistently demonstrate a statistically significant superiority of PPIs over placebo. 35 The landmark Cochrane review by Pinto-Sanchez et al. 9 quantifies this benefit, reporting a NNT for benefit of 11, highlighting that while PPIs are effective, a substantial proportion of patients do not achieve adequate symptom relief with monotherapy. Given the acid-suppressive mechanism of PPIs, researchers have specifically investigated whether their efficacy differs between the EPS and PDS subtypes. Clinical trials assessing global symptom relief demonstrated that PPIs can be effective in both EPS and PDS populations, and there was a lack of robust evidence suggesting different response rates between the two subtypes. 36 However, when symptoms were evaluated separately, a clear gradient of benefit emerges. The most robust and consistent improvements are observed in epigastric pain and burning, the hallmark symptoms of EPS. In contrast, the effect on core PDS symptoms—postprandial fullness and early satiation—is typically less pronounced. 37 This differential efficacy can be attributed to the distinct symptom profiles of the two subtypes. The relief of epigastric pain and burning in EPS patients aligns directly with the acid-suppressive mechanism of PPIs. In PDS patients, while a reduction in overlapping upper abdominal discomfort may occur, the core symptoms of postprandial fullness and early satiation are primarily driven by other mechanisms.

PPIs provide significantly greater efficacy in acid suppression when compared with H2RAs, another class of acid-suppressive agents. An RCT demonstrated that the rate of complete symptom relief was significantly higher with omeprazole than with ranitidine in patients infected with H. pylori . 38 This superior efficacy may be attributed to the more profound and sustained acid suppression achieved with PPIs. 9 , 38 In addition, the rapid development of tolerance associated with H2RAs can limit their long-term efficacy; such tolerance is not commonly observed with PPIs. 39 Nevertheless, H2RAs remain valuable in specific scenarios, such as for on-demand therapy or for patients who experience severe adverse effects from PPIs, due to their distinct pharmacological profile.

Comparisons with other pharmacologic classes further refine the role of PPIs in the management hierarchy. Accumulating evidence indicates that PPIs may offer a modest advantage over prokinetics in terms of overall symptom improvement. 9 , 40 , 41 However, such findings warrant cautious interpretation. When analyzed by subtype, a different pattern emerges: among patients with predominant PDS symptoms, the therapeutic benefit of PPIs is attenuated, and prokinetics show comparable efficacy in alleviating meal-related symptoms. 42 This nuanced evidence has led to divergent recommendations across major international guidelines. For instance, guidelines in the United Kingdom and Japan recommend prokinetics as a first-line empirical option alongside PPIs for FD. 7 , 8 In contrast, the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) guideline advocates a sequential strategy, suggesting prokinetics only after failure of PPIs or tricyclic antidepressants. 34 These divergent positions on prokinetics may stem from pragmatic differences in drug availability, the regional strength of evidence, and distinct safety landscapes. The Japanese guideline’s strong endorsement of prokinetics, specifically acotiamide, is supported by robust domestic RCT evidence for a drug approved and widely used locally. In contrast, the 2017 ACG guideline, formulated in a context where many prokinetics are unavailable (e.g., acotiamide) 43 , 44 or carry notable safety concerns (e.g., metoclopramide), and where the overall evidence from randomized trials was judged to be of very low quality, logically adopts a more conservative sequential strategy. The UK guideline reflects an intermediate, pragmatic stance, acknowledging potential efficacy but explicitly noting limited availability outside specific regions and variable evidence quality. This variation underscores a consistent limitation: the evidence base for prokinetics remains fragmented, often region-specific, and lacking large-scale, high-quality multinational trials that could support a unified, strong global recommendation.

Consequently, in the current therapeutic landscape, PPIs maintain their role as the most universally applicable, evidence-backed first-line pharmacological cornerstone for FD, due to their broader availability, more consistent efficacy data across diverse populations, and extensively documented safety profile. Although emerging data suggest a potential gradient of efficacy with greater benefit observed in patients with EPS, these findings remain preliminary and require validation through prospective, symptom-subtype-specific clinical trials. Overall, PPI therapy constitutes an effective, evidence-based first-line approach in the empirical treatment of FD across a broad patient population, while acknowledging the need for further research to identify reliable predictors of treatment response, especially in relation to distinct symptom clusters.

Recently, potassium-competitive acid blockers (P-CABs) have emerged as a new class of acid-suppressive agents that address several pharmacological limitations of PPIs. Unlike PPIs, which require acid activation and bind irreversibly to actively pumping H+/ K+-ATPase pumps, P-CABs act as potassium-competitive inhibitors. Emerging clinical evidence has begun to substantiate their role in FD. A multi-center study by Huh et al. 45 revealed that 74.6% and 86.7% of participants receiving tegoprazan achieved satisfactory symptom relief at weeks 4 and 8, respectively. The efficacy of tegoprazan was not influenced by the FD subtype or H. pylori status. Furthermore, researchers have found that P-CABs were effective in patients with FD who had inadequate symptom control with PPI treatment. An RCT revealed that vonoprazan can improve quality of life and dyspepsia symptoms, with a response rate of 75.9% at week 8. 46 While P-CABs show promise, their superiority over PPIs in FD has not been established and requires further validation, particularly through head-to-head comparisons.

NON-ACID-SUPPRESSIVE EFFECTS OF PPIs IN FD The therapeutic benefits of PPIs in FD have traditionally been ascribed solely to the reduction of acid exposure. However, a growing body of evidence suggests that PPIs exert a range of effects beyond acid suppression. These novel mechanisms include immunomodulation, alteration of the gut microbiota, and consequential impacts on intestinal barrier function.

ANTI-INFLAMMATORY AND EOSINOPHIL-REDUCING EFFECTS PPIs have been shown to exhibit direct anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, with one key emerging mechanism being their ability to reduce eosinophil levels. Eosinophils have been recognized as critical contributors to FD, inducing duodenal micro-inflammation and promoting sensitization of adjacent neurons, 26 especially in those with PDS. 47 Elevated eosinophil numbers and degranulation have been observed in FD. 48 A clinical study by Wauters et al. 10 has shown that pantoprazole not only alleviates symptoms but also reduces duodenal eosinophils and mast cell counts, as well as epithelial permeability. Furthermore, these eosinophil-reducing effects were associated with clinical improvement in FD patients. By attenuating the eosinophil-mediated inflammation and the consequent neuronal sensitization, PPIs may alleviate visceral hypersensitivity.

Beyond eosinophils, PPIs demonstrate antioxidant properties by scavenging oxygen free radicals and suppressing reactive oxygen species production in neutrophils and macrophages. Moreover, PPIs reduce the expression of inflammatory mediators in these cells, thereby inhibiting chemotaxis, migration, and phagocytic activity. 49 Additionally, certain PPIs can induce neutrophil apoptosis through enhanced mitochondrial stress resulting from proteasomal inhibition and accumulation of unfolded proteins. 50 Collectively, these mechanisms contribute to the attenuation of the low-grade inflammation observed in some patients with FD. However, this immunomodulatory effect may compromise host defense and increase infection risk, as evidenced by the inhibition of interleukin (IL)-1β secretion reported by Hinoki et al. 51

MODULATION OF THE GUT MICROBIOTA The profound increase in gastric pH caused by PPIs significantly alters the gastrointestinal microenvironment, leading to marked changes in the composition and function of the gut microbiota. This dysbiosis is not merely an incidental observation but is increasingly recognized as an active contributor to the symptomatology of FD, establishing a complex interplay between pharmacological treatment, microbial ecology, and disease pathogenesis. The gastric acid barrier acts as a critical gatekeeper, effectively limiting the passage of orally ingested bacteria into the lower gastrointestinal tract. By elevating intragastric pH, PPIs compromise this barrier, facilitating the survival and passage of microorganisms into the gastrointestinal tract. This results in two primary phenomena: small intestinal bacterial overgrowth and a shift in the colonic microbiota toward an oropharyngeal-like composition, especially a consistently observed increase in Streptococcus abundance. 52 - 55

Although there are no direct reports on how altered microbiota influence dyspeptic symptoms, increasing evidence suggests several possibilities. For example, recent evidence suggests that Streptococcus species may play dual roles in modulating mucosal immune responses within the duodenum, depending on strain-specific characteristics, relative abundance, and host immune status. Certain Streptococcus isolates, through surface molecules such as peptidoglycan and lipoteichoic acids, can activate pattern recognition receptors (e.g., TLR2 and TLR4) on epithelial and immune cells, promoting NF-κB signaling and the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines including tumor necrosis factor-α, IL-1β, and IL-8, which may contribute to low-grade mucosal inflammation. 56 - 58 Overrepresentation of Streptococcus in the upper small intestine could further exacerbate immune activation by disrupting epithelial tight junctions and altering microbial homeostasis, favoring a proinflammatory environment. 59 , 60 Conversely, several Streptococcus species, notably S. thermophilus and other commensal or probiotic strains, have demonstrated immunomodulatory potential by inducing regulatory cytokines such as IL-10, attenuating inflammatory signaling, and supporting mucosal tolerance. 61 These contrasting effects underscore the context-dependent nature of Streptococcus -host interactions. A balanced colonization may maintain immune homeostasis, whereas dysregulated proliferation or the presence of more immunogenic strains could drive subtle, persistent inflammatory signaling in the duodenal mucosa.

It is crucial to distinguish between the direct pharmacologic actions of PPIs and the indirect consequences of profound acid suppression when considering their mechanisms of action in FD. The modulation of the gut microbiota discussed here is predominantly an indirect effect, a consequence of the elevation of intragastric pH. By disabling the gastric acid barrier, PPIs alter the ecological niche for microorganisms throughout the upper GI tract, facilitating bacterial survival, overgrowth, and compositional shifts. Therefore, while microbial changes may contribute to the symptom landscape in FD, they are primarily downstream of PPIs’ core acid-suppressive action. In contrast, anti-inflammatory effects such as the reduction of duodenal eosinophils appear to represent more direct pharmacologic properties of PPIs, potentially independent of pH elevation. Thus, symptom improvement with PPI therapy likely results from a combination of direct acid suppression, anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory effects, and indirect, acid-mediated alterations in the gut microenvironment and microbiota, which may in turn influence mucosal immunity and neural signaling. Further studies are warranted to elucidate the mechanistic link between PPI-mediated microbial shifts and the clinical manifestations of FD, especially regarding the potential functional roles of distinct Streptococcus taxa.

ENHANCED INTESTINAL PERMEABILITY Apart from the dysbiosis-induced disruption of epithelial tight junctions, emerging research suggests that long-term PPI use may be directly associated with enhanced intestinal permeability. An insightful study by Nighot et al. 62 has elucidated a molecular pathway through which long-term PPI use compromises gut barrier integrity. PPIs, by elevating the extracellular pH, can activate the p38 MAPK signaling pathway. This leads to the upregulation of myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) expression and activity. MLCK is a central regulator of tight junction permeability; its activation triggers the phosphorylation of myosin light chains, causing contraction of the peri-junctional actin-myosin ring and physical opening of the tight junctions.

A compromised intestinal barrier allows the translocation of luminal antigens, bacteria, and their products into the mucosal lamina propria. This breach sustains local immune activation and low-grade inflammation, a key pathophysiological feature in FD. Therefore, while PPIs may alleviate symptoms in the short term by reducing acid, their long-term use might inadvertently perpetuate the cycle of symptom generation in a subset of patients by damaging the very barrier that protects the gut from immune triggers.

SUMMARY This comprehensive review affirms that PPIs remain a cornerstone in the management of FD. The evidence demonstrates a consistent, albeit modest, superiority of PPIs over placebo and a generally favorable profile compared to other first-line pharmacologic classes like H2RAs and prokinetics. Beyond this established efficacy, our understanding of PPI action in FD has evolved significantly. It is now clear that their therapeutic role involves multiple mechanisms beyond simple acid suppression, such as the modulation of duodenal immune responses—notably the reduction of eosinophils and mast cells—and the dampening of low-grade inflammation.

These mechanistic insights hold immediate and future implications for clinical practice. The anti-inflammatory properties of PPIs, particularly their ability to reduce duodenal eosinophils, provide a potential path toward a more stratified treatment approach. For instance, the presence of duodenal eosinophilia could, in the future, serve as a predictive biomarker to identify a patient subgroup most likely to derive significant benefit from PPI therapy, moving beyond the current symptom-based classification.

However, this review also highlights a critical complexity: the same profound alteration of the gastrointestinal environment that may contribute to efficacy also drives potential adverse long-term consequences, including significant gut microbiota dysbiosis and MLCK-mediated increases in intestinal permeability. This complexity calls for a more nuanced approach to long-term PPI management. While the clinical relevance of these effects in the FD population is not yet fully quantified, they offer a plausible explanation for the phenomenon of diminishing returns or symptom recurrence in some patients on prolonged PPI therapy. Such links require further research to be fully elucidated.

In conclusion, PPIs remain an indispensable and evidence-based first-line therapy for FD, with their position solidified by proven efficacy and newly discovered anti-inflammatory properties. However, their application should be guided by predominant symptom phenotype, and clinicians must be mindful of the potential for long-term pathophysiological consequences alongside the short-term symptomatic benefits. The future of acid suppression in FD lies in refining patient selection, understanding the full spectrum of drug actions, and embracing novel agents that may offer improved therapeutic profiles. Background and Objectives : Functional dyspepsia (FD) is a heterogeneous disorder of gut–brain interaction with a multifactorial pathophysiology. Although Helicobacter pylori infection has been implicated in FD, its relationship with Rome IV FD subgroups and the extent to which successful eradication results in sustained symptomatic improvement remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate the distribution of H. pylori infection across Rome IV FD subgroups and to assess long-term symptomatic response following successful eradication. Materials and Methods : This prospective, single-center observational cohort study included patients with dyspeptic symptoms who underwent evaluation according to the Rome IV criteria. Adult patients who completed the Rome IV gastroduodenal symptom questionnaire and underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy were evaluated. Patients fulfilling the Rome IV criteria for FD without an organic cause explaining their symptoms were classified as postprandial distress syndrome (PDS), epigastric pain syndrome (EPS), or overlapping PDS–EPS. H. pylori status was determined histopathologically using gastric antral and corpus biopsies. H. pylori -positive patients received 14-day bismuth-based quadruple therapy, and eradication was assessed using a stool antigen test 8–12 weeks after treatment. Symptomatic response was evaluated at month 2, 6, and 12 using Likert scale and clinical assessment. Results : Of 425 patients evaluated, 244 fulfilled the Rome IV criteria for FD, and 127 (52.0%) were H. pylori positive. The prevalence of H. pylori infection differed significantly among the Rome IV FD subgroups ( p < 0.001) and was highest in the EPS subgroup (73.4%, 58/79), compared with the PDS (37.7%, 40/106) and overlapping (49.2%, 29/59) subgroups. H. pylori positivity was significantly higher in EPS than in both PDS and overlapping subgroups ( p < 0.001 and p = 0.003, respectively). First-line eradication rates were 96.4% (106/110) per protocol and 83.5% (106/127) by intention to treat. Symptomatic response rates following successful eradication were 43.4% (46/106), 60.4% (64/106), and 70.2% (66/94) at month 2, 6, and 12, respectively, compared with 47.0% (55/117), 63.4% (71/112), and 78.4% (80/102) in H. pylori -negative patients. Between-group differences in symptomatic response were not statistically significant ( p = 0.58, 0.64, and 0.18, respectively). In the conservative sensitivity analysis, month 12 response was lower in the H. pylori -positive cohort (55.1% vs. 68.4%, p = 0.03). Sustained complete symptom resolution occurred in 25.5% (24/94) of patients after successful eradication and 19.6% (20/102) of H. pylori -negative patients ( p = 0.32). Conclusions : H. pylori infection was significantly more prevalent in the EPS phenotype, supporting the biological heterogeneity of Rome IV functional dyspepsia. Sustained complete symptom resolution occurred in 25.5% after successful eradication and 19.6% in the H. pylori -negative cohort. Despite successful eradication in 96.4% per protocol and 83.5% by intention to treat, no clear symptomatic advantage over the H. pylori -negative cohort was demonstrated. Introduction Functional dyspepsia (FD) is one of the most common functional gastrointestinal disorders, with a recent systematic review and meta-analysis reporting a global pooled prevalence of 8.4%, which decreased to 6.8% when the Rome IV criteria were applied. It negatively affects quality of life and daily functioning, leading to increased healthcare utilization, reduced work productivity, and a substantial economic burden [ 1 , 2 ]. However, the pathogenesis of FD remains incompletely understood, and multiple mechanisms, including visceral hypersensitivity, gastroduodenal motility disturbances, low-grade inflammation, alterations in the gut–brain axis, and Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection, are thought to contribute to its pathogenesis [ 3 ].

According to the Rome IV criteria, functional dyspepsia is classified into two main subgroups: postprandial distress syndrome (PDS) and epigastric pain syndrome (EPS). The substantial overlap between PDS and EPS observed with the Rome III criteria has been markedly reduced with the Rome IV criteria, allowing for the identification of more homogeneous patient groups [ 2 ]. This distinction has also raised the possibility that different FD subgroups may involve distinct pathophysiological mechanisms. In particular, the weaker association of symptoms with meals in the EPS subgroup suggests that different mechanisms may underlie the clinical manifestations of these subgroups [ 2 ].

In recent years, functional gastrointestinal disorders have increasingly been reconsidered within the framework of disorders of gut–brain interaction, with growing emphasis on the need to complement symptom-based classifications with underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Therefore, studies investigating the distribution of H. pylori infection across Rome IV subgroups may contribute to a better characterization of the biological subtypes of functional dyspepsia and may help inform future classification systems [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ].

Helicobacter pylori is a common infectious agent affecting approximately half of the global population and is considered one of the factors potentially involved in the pathogenesis of functional dyspepsia [ 5 , 6 ]. Current evidence indicates that eradication therapy in H. pylori -positive patients with functional dyspepsia provides a significant but modest improvement in dyspeptic symptoms. The concept of “ H. pylori -associated dyspepsia” was introduced by the Kyoto global consensus and subsequently adopted by Rome IV, referring to sustained symptom resolution following successful H. pylori eradication [ 7 ].

This distinction makes it challenging to differentiate “ H. pylori -associated dyspepsia” from “functional dyspepsia,” particularly in regions where H. pylori infection is endemic, and complicates terminological classification. Furthermore, establishing this distinction and confirming a diagnosis of functional dyspepsia requires a prolonged follow-up period.

However, the relationship between H. pylori infection and the functional dyspepsia subgroups defined by the Rome IV criteria has not been sufficiently investigated. Particularly in populations with a high prevalence of H. pylori , it remains unclear whether the distribution of infection differs between the EPS and PDS subgroups and whether these subgroups differ in their response to eradication therapy. Türkiye, where the prevalence of H. pylori has been reported to range from 65% to 82.5%, represents a suitable population in which to investigate these associations [ 8 , 9 ].

Therefore, characterizing the distribution of H. pylori infection across subgroups of patients with functional dyspepsia defined according to the Rome IV criteria may contribute to a better understanding of the biological heterogeneity of functional dyspepsia, facilitate the refinement of current terminology, and support the development of more targeted therapeutic strategies. These findings may also provide insights that could inform future revisions of the Rome classification system. The aim of this study was to evaluate the prevalence of H. pylori infection among functional dyspepsia subgroups classified according to the Rome IV criteria in a population with a high prevalence of H. pylori and to assess long-term symptomatic response following successful eradication in comparison with H. pylori -negative patients. In addition, we aimed to determine the association of H. pylori infection with the EPS and PDS subtypes and to assess the frequency of sustained complete symptom resolution after successful eradication.

2. Material and Methods 2.1. Study Population Our study was a single-center, prospective observational cohort study that included patients diagnosed with functional dyspepsia according to the Rome IV criteria among those who underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy at the Gastroenterology Department of Sakarya University Faculty of Medicine, Sakarya Training and Research Hospital, between January 2023 and January 2025.

Patients aged 18 years or older with a preliminary diagnosis of functional dyspepsia who presented to our clinic with dyspeptic symptoms and were scheduled for upper gastrointestinal endoscopy completed the Rome IV gastroduodenal symptom questionnaire before the procedure, and a detailed medical history was obtained. Subsequently, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was performed, and biopsy specimens were obtained for histopathological assessment of H. pylori . All endoscopic procedures were performed by gastroenterologists experienced in endoscopy. A standardized gastric biopsy protocol was used in accordance with ESGE recommendations, with two biopsies obtained from the antrum and two from the corpus, preferentially sampling areas with visible mucosal abnormalities. Biopsy specimens were evaluated using hematoxylin–eosin and Giemsa staining, with immunohistochemistry used in equivocal cases. H. pylori positivity was defined by the histological identification of organisms consistent with H. pylori . As all patients underwent endoscopy to exclude organic causes of dyspepsia, baseline H. pylori status was determined histologically using gastric biopsies obtained during the same procedure; a second diagnostic test was not routinely performed.

Functional dyspepsia was diagnosed according to the Rome IV criteria, and patients were classified as having postprandial distress syndrome (PDS), epigastric pain syndrome (EPS), or PDS–EPS overlap according to the Rome IV subgroup criteria.

Patients who incompletely or inadequately completed the Rome IV questionnaire or had incomplete clinical assessments; individuals younger than 18 years; pregnant or breastfeeding women; patients with organic gastrointestinal pathology on upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, including peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, or Los Angeles grade B or higher esophagitis; those with a history of diabetes mellitus, depression or anxiety, celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or upper gastrointestinal surgery; regular users of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or acetylsalicylic acid; patients with predominant symptoms suggestive of other gastrointestinal disorders, including gastroesophageal reflux disease, dysphagia, globus sensation, or irritable bowel syndrome; those who had received H. pylori eradication therapy within the preceding three months; and patients without informed consent were excluded from the study. In addition, to minimize the risk of false-negative results related to medications that could reduce the sensitivity of histopathological assessment, patients who had used proton pump inhibitors within two weeks or antibiotics or bismuth preparations within four weeks before endoscopy were excluded.

Before treatment, all patients received counseling on lifestyle modifications and dietary recommendations. H. pylori -positive patients received a 14-day bismuth-containing quadruple eradication regimen consisting of esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily, bismuth 500 mg four times daily, metronidazole 500 mg three times daily, and tetracycline 500 mg four times daily. Patients in whom eradication was unsuccessful after first-line therapy received a second-line eradication regimen consisting of esomeprazole 40 mg twice daily, bismuth 500 mg four times daily, levofloxacin 500 mg once daily, and tetracycline 500 mg four times daily. In patients who completed the treatment regimen as prescribed, eradication success was assessed 8–12 weeks after treatment using a stool H. pylori antigen test. Before testing, patients were required to have discontinued antibiotics, bismuth preparations, proton pump inhibitors, antacids, and histamine receptor antagonists for at least two weeks. A second diagnostic method, such as a rapid urease test, serology, or urea breath test, was not routinely used to determine H. pylori status. Patients who were unable to complete the 14-day eradication regimen or in whom successful eradication could not be confirmed by the stool H. pylori antigen test were not included in the symptomatic response analysis of patients who achieved successful eradication.

Gastroesophageal reflux symptoms were assessed separately during the clinical evaluation and symptom assessment. Heartburn was distinguished from epigastric burning based on the anatomical location of the symptom. A burning sensation perceived in the retrosternal region or extending from the epigastric to the retrosternal region was considered heartburn, whereas burning localized to the epigastric region without retrosternal extension was considered epigastric burning within the Rome IV framework. The presence of regurgitation was assessed separately and was considered a symptom supportive of gastroesophageal reflux. Patients with isolated heartburn and/or regurgitation were not included in the functional dyspepsia cohort. At this stage, symptom-based diagnostic assessment and assignment to the appropriate functional dyspepsia subgroup were determined by experienced gastroenterologists. Patients with Los Angeles grade B or higher esophagitis on endoscopic evaluation were excluded from the study, whereas grade A esophagitis alone was not considered an exclusion criterion.

In the H. pylori -negative group, patients with EPS-predominant symptoms received a proton pump inhibitor once daily for 4–8 weeks, whereas those with PDS-predominant symptoms received a prokinetic agent for 4–8 weeks. Patients meeting both PDS and EPS criteria remained classified as overlap; treatment was selected according to the predominant symptom and continued for 4–8 weeks.

Follow-up visits were scheduled at months 2, 6, and 12 from treatment initiation (month 0), defined as the date eradication therapy or H. pylori -negative medical treatment was initiated after review of the histopathology report. At each follow-up visit, symptomatic response was assessed based on the symptoms defining the functional dyspepsia subgroup to which each patient had been assigned at baseline. Patients were asked whether the symptoms corresponding to their respective subgroup remained bothersome to an extent that interfered with their daily activities, and responses were recorded using a four-point Likert-type scale. In patients with PDS or EPS, the symptoms defining the respective subgroup were evaluated, whereas in patients with the overlap phenotype, all symptoms defining both PDS and EPS were assessed. Symptomatic response was defined as a response of “strongly disagree” (Likert 1) or “disagree” (Likert 2) to the statement “My bothersome symptoms persist” for all symptoms evaluated. If a response of Likert 3 or 4 was recorded for any symptom, the patient was classified as a symptomatic non-responder. This approach was used as the operational definition of symptomatic response in our study to determine whether the symptoms defining the Rome IV phenotype remained bothersome enough to interfere with daily activities during follow-up. Thus, symptomatic response was defined as a binary endpoint based on the combined assessment of all symptoms constituting the patient’s functional dyspepsia phenotype.

Complete symptom resolution was defined as a Likert score of 1 for all relevant subgroup-defining symptoms. Among patients with successful H. pylori eradication who completed both visits, meeting this criterion at months 6 and 12 constituted the study’s operational definition of sustained complete symptom resolution after eradication. The same criterion of sustained complete symptom resolution (Likert 1 for all relevant symptoms at both months 6 and 12) was applied to H. pylori -negative patients who completed both visits, and the proportions were compared between cohorts.

The primary endpoint of the study was to compare the prevalence of H. pylori infection across functional dyspepsia subgroups classified according to the Rome IV criteria. The secondary endpoint was to compare symptomatic response rates at month 2, month 6, and month 12 between two patient groups: those who achieved successful H. pylori eradication and those who were H. pylori -negative at baseline. In the primary analysis, symptomatic response was evaluated among patients who completed consecutive follow-up visits; patients who missed a follow-up visit were not re-included in the primary analysis at subsequent time points.

Cochran’s Q test was used to evaluate changes in symptomatic response over time within each group. To ensure that paired analyses were performed on the same individuals, this analysis was restricted to patients with available symptomatic response data at all three follow-up time points (month 2, month 6, and month 12). Following a significant Cochran’s Q test, pairwise comparisons between time points were performed using the McNemar test.

To assess potential bias related to loss to follow-up and the evaluation of patients who achieved successful eradication, a conservative sensitivity analysis was performed including the entire baseline H. pylori -positive ( n = 127) and H. pylori -negative ( n = 117) cohorts. All patients were retained in their respective baseline cohorts, and available symptomatic response data at month 2, month 6, and month 12 were used. Patients without symptomatic response data at a given follow-up time point were conservatively classified as non-responders. Thus, the same approach to missing follow-up data was applied to both cohorts. In addition, to assess whether loss to follow-up was selective, patients who completed follow-up and those who did not were compared with respect to baseline age, sex, and functional dyspepsia phenotype.

2.2. Definitions Functional dyspepsia was defined according to the Rome IV diagnostic criteria as the presence of at least one dyspeptic symptom during the preceding three months, with symptom onset at least six months before diagnosis, in the absence of structural disease that could explain the symptoms, including findings on upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Dyspeptic symptoms included at least one of the following bothersome symptoms: postprandial fullness, early satiation, epigastric pain, and/or epigastric burning. The diagnosis of functional dyspepsia was established when the Rome IV diagnostic criteria were fully met and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed no organic pathology that could explain the symptoms.

Patients diagnosed with functional dyspepsia were classified into three subgroups according to the Rome IV criteria: postprandial distress syndrome (PDS), epigastric pain syndrome (EPS), and PDS–EPS overlap. Among patients fulfilling the relevant criteria, those with bothersome postprandial fullness and/or early satiation at least three days per week were classified as PDS, whereas those with epigastric pain and/or epigastric burning at least one day per week were classified as EPS. Patients who fulfilled the symptom criteria for both PDS and EPS were classified as having PDS–EPS overlap.

2.3. Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 23.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). Categorical variables were expressed as numbers and percentages, whereas continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation. The independent-samples t-test was used to compare continuous variables between two groups, and Pearson’s chi-square test was used for comparisons of categorical variables. Bonferroni correction was applied for pairwise comparisons among functional dyspepsia subgroups. Cochran’s Q test was used to compare symptomatic response rates at month 2, month 6, and month 12 within the same patient group, and when a statistically significant difference was detected, pairwise comparisons were performed using the McNemar test. Effect sizes for between-group comparisons of categorical outcomes were reported as absolute differences in prevalence or symptomatic response rates, together with their 95% confidence intervals. For the three post hoc pairwise comparisons, Bonferroni correction was applied, with the threshold for statistical significance set at p < 0.0167. A p -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all other analyses. Longitudinal symptomatic response was evaluated using logistic generalized estimating equations (GEE) with an exchangeable correlation structure and robust standard errors. The model included group, categorical time, a group × time interaction, and baseline FD phenotype (PDS, EPS, or overlap) as a categorical covariate to assess whether response trajectories differed between cohorts after adjustment for phenotype. A power assessment was also performed for the secondary endpoint. Based on the available sample sizes at each follow-up time point, the minimum detectable absolute between-group differences were calculated assuming a two-sided α of 0.05 and 80% power. The minimum detectable differences were approximately 18.6%, 18.3%, and 17.3% at month 2, month 6, and month 12, respectively.

3. Results A total of 425 patients who completed the Rome IV gastroduodenal symptom questionnaire and underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy for dyspeptic symptoms were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 181 patients were excluded because they did not meet the study criteria. Eighty-seven patients were excluded because upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed peptic ulcer disease, malignancy, Los Angeles (LA) grade B or higher esophagitis, or anatomical changes related to previous gastric surgery. An additional 43 patients were excluded because of the previously specified chronic diseases. Thirty-nine patients were excluded because their symptom profiles were not compatible with the study criteria; among these, 16 had predominant gastroesophageal reflux symptoms, including regurgitation and/or retrosternal burning (heartburn). In addition, 12 patients were excluded because of previous H. pylori eradication therapy or the use of medications that could affect the histopathological assessment of H. pylori . After all exclusions, 244 patients were included in the final study cohort. Los Angeles grade A esophagitis was identified in three patients (1.2%; 3/244) in the final cohort (The study flow diagram is presented in Figure 1 ).

The mean age of patients diagnosed with functional dyspepsia according to the Rome IV criteria was 39.8 ± 13.3 years; 61.1% (149/244) were female and 38.9% (95/244) were male. Regarding functional dyspepsia subgroups, 43.4% (106/244) of patients were classified as having postprandial distress syndrome (PDS), 32.4% (79/244) as having epigastric pain syndrome (EPS), and 24.2% (59/244) as having PDS–EPS overlap. Histopathological examination revealed H. pylori positivity in 52.0% (127/244) of the 244 patients diagnosed with functional dyspepsia. Among H. pylori -positive patients, 59.1% (75/127) were female, and the mean age was 39.8 ± 12.9 years. Among the 117 H. pylori -negative patients, 63.2% (74/117) were female, and the mean age was 39.9 ± 13.7 years. There were no statistically significant differences between the H. pylori -positive and H. pylori -negative groups in terms of age ( p = 0.95) or sex distribution ( p = 0.51). Smoking was reported in 26.8% ( n = 34) of H. pylori -positive patients and 24.8% ( n = 29) of H. pylori -negative patients. Social alcohol consumption was reported in 16.5% ( n = 21) and 12.8% ( n = 15) of patients, respectively.

Among the 127 H. pylori -positive patients, 45.7% ( n = 58) were classified as EPS, 31.5% ( n = 40) as PDS, and 22.8% ( n = 29) as PDS–EPS overlap. In contrast, among the 117 H. pylori -negative patients, 56.4% ( n = 66) were classified as PDS, 17.9% ( n = 21) as EPS, and 25.6% ( n = 30) as PDS–EPS overlap. The prevalence of H. pylori infection differed significantly across the functional dyspepsia subgroups ( p < 0.001). The prevalence of H. pylori infection was 73.4% (58/79) in the EPS subgroup, 37.7% (40/106) in the PDS subgroup, and 49.2% (29/59) in the PDS–EPS overlap subgroup. H. pylori prevalence was significantly higher in the EPS subgroup than in the PDS subgroup (95% CI for the absolute difference, 22.3–49.1%; p < 0.001) and the PDS–EPS overlap subgroup (95% CI for the absolute difference, 8.2–40.3%; p = 0.003). The difference between the PDS and PDS–EPS overlap subgroups was not statistically significant (absolute difference, −11.4%; 95% CI, −27.2% to 4.3%; p = 0.15) (the demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population are presented in Table 1 ).

Multivariable logistic regression was performed with baseline H. pylori positivity as the dependent variable and FD phenotype, age, sex, smoking, and alcohol consumption as explanatory variables. After adjustment for age, sex, smoking, and alcohol consumption, EPS remained associated with H. pylori positivity compared with PDS (aOR, 4.83; 95% CI, 2.53–9.21; p < 0.001) and overlap (aOR, 3.03; 95% CI, 1.47–6.24; p = 0.003).

Of the 127 H. pylori -positive patients, five declined eradication therapy, while six discontinued treatment because of adverse effects. The remaining 116 patients completed the eradication regimen. During follow-up, eradication success was assessed in 110 of these 116 patients using the stool H. pylori antigen test. First-line eradication rates were 96.4% (106/110) per protocol and 83.5% (106/127) by intention to treat. The five patients who declined eradication therapy and the six patients who were unable to complete treatment because of adverse effects received a standard-dose proton pump inhibitor for four weeks, whereas the six patients in whom eradication status could not be assessed received no additional treatment. The four patients in whom first-line eradication therapy failed received second-line eradication therapy, with successful eradication achieved in all four patients.

During follow-up, additional rescue treatments were administered for persistent or recurrent dyspeptic symptoms. Among patients who achieved successful H. pylori eradication, 26 (24.5%; 26/106) received a proton pump inhibitor once daily for four weeks at month 2, and 12 (11.3%; 12/106) received the same treatment at month 6. In the H. pylori -negative cohort, 32 patients (27.4%; 32/117) at month 2 and 8 patients (7.1%; 8/112) at month 6 received an additional four-week course of rescue therapy. Treatment was selected according to the functional dyspepsia phenotype, with a proton pump inhibitor once daily for patients with EPS and a prokinetic agent for those with PDS. No additional rescue treatment was administered in either cohort at month 12. Initial and rescue treatments in the H. pylori -negative cohort are summarized in Supplementary Table S1 .

In the analysis group comprising patients who achieved successful H. pylori eradication and H. pylori -negative patients, symptomatic response rates at month 2, month 6, and month 12 were 45.3% (101/223), 61.9% (135/218), and 74.5% (146/196), respectively. Among patients who achieved successful H. pylori eradication, symptomatic response rates at month 2, month 6, and month 12 were 43.4% (46/106), 60.4% (64/106), and 70.2% (66/94), respectively. Among H. pylori -negative patients, symptomatic response rates were 47.0% (55/117), 63.4% (71/112), and 78.4% (80/102) at month 2, month 6, and month 12, respectively. Of the 21 H. pylori -positive patients who were not included in the successful-eradication cohort after first-line treatment, 15 attended the month 2 follow-up visit, 9 attended the month 6 visit, and 4 attended the month 12 visit. Symptomatic response rates among these patients were 33.3% (5/15), 55.6% (5/9), and 100% (4/4), respectively.

Symptomatic response rates among H. pylori -positive patients who achieved successful eradication and H. pylori -negative patients were 43.4% (46/106) and 47.0% (55/117), respectively, at month 2 (absolute difference, −3.6%; 95% CI, −16.7% to 9.5%; p = 0.58); 60.4% (64/106) and 63.4% (71/112), respectively, at month 6 (absolute difference, −3.0%; 95% CI, −15.9% to 9.9%; p = 0.64); and 70.2% (66/94) and 78.4% (80/102), respectively, at month 12 (absolute difference, −8.2%; 95% CI, −20.4% to 4.0%; p = 0.18). No statistically significant differences between the groups were observed at any follow-up time point (Symptomatic response rates during follow-up are presented in Table 2 ).

All 106 patients who achieved successful eradication completed the month 2 and month 6 follow-up visits, whereas 11.3% (12/106) did not attend the month 12 follow-up visit. In the H. pylori -negative group, 4.3% (5/117) of patients did not attend the month 6 follow-up visit, and an additional 8.9% (10/112) did not attend the month 12 follow-up visit. No statistically significant differences in baseline age or sex were observed between patients who completed follow-up and those who did not (age, p = 0.65; sex, p = 0.52). Similarly, the baseline distribution of functional dyspepsia phenotypes was comparable between patients who completed and those who did not complete the 12-month follow-up in both the successful-eradication cohort and the H. pylori -negative cohort ( p = 0.86).

The 94 patients in the successful-eradication cohort and 102 H. pylori -negative patients with available symptomatic response data at all three follow-up visits were included in the within-group longitudinal analysis. In the successful-eradication cohort, symptomatic response rates at month 2, month 6, and month 12 were 40.4% (38/94), 57.4% (54/94), and 70.2% (66/94), respectively, showing a significant increase over time (Cochran’s Q = 38.19; p < 0.001). Similarly, in the H. pylori -negative cohort, symptomatic response rates were 42.2% (43/102), 63.7% (65/102), and 78.4% (80/102), respectively, with a significant increase over time (Cochran’s Q = 49.48; p < 0.001). In Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc McNemar analyses, significant differences were observed for all comparisons between month 2 and month 6, month 2 and month 12, and month 6 and month 12 in both cohorts (successful-eradication cohort: p < 0.001, p < 0.001, and p = 0.006, respectively; H. pylori -negative cohort: p < 0.001, p < 0.001, and p = 0.001, respectively).

In the conservative sensitivity analysis, in which the entire baseline cohorts were retained and patients without follow-up data were classified as non-responders, symptomatic response rates in the H. pylori -positive and H. pylori -negative cohorts were 40.2% (51/127) and 47.0% (55/117), respectively, at month 2 (absolute difference, −6.9%; 95% CI, −19.3% to 5.6%; p = 0.28); 54.3% (69/127) and 60.7% (71/117), respectively, at month 6 (absolute difference, −6.4%; 95% CI, −18.7% to 6.0%; p = 0.31); and 55.1% (70/127) and 68.4% (80/117), respectively, at month 12 (absolute difference, −13.3%; 95% CI, −25.3% to −1.2%; p = 0.03). No statistically significant difference was observed at the first two time points, whereas symptomatic response at month 12 was significantly higher in the H. pylori -negative cohort. The GEE analysis included 223 patients and 637 observations. Symptomatic response rates by baseline FD phenotype within each cohort are presented in Table 3 . After adjustment for phenotype, the group × time interaction remained non-significant (Wald χ 2 = 1.07; df = 2; p = 0.59). In the LOCF sensitivity analysis, which carried the last available response forward and retained patients without any follow-up data as non-responders, month 12 response rates were 66.9% (85/127) and 76.1% (89/117), respectively ( p = 0.115).

Among the 94 patients who achieved successful H. pylori eradication and completed both the month 6 and month 12 follow-up visits, 24 (25.5%) had complete symptom resolution (Likert = 1) at both time points. These 24 patients represented 22.6% of the primary successful-eradication cohort (24/106) and 18.9% of the baseline H. pylori -positive cohort (24/127). Thirty-three patients were not included in this classification: 21 were outside the primary successful-eradication cohort, and 12 lacked month 12 follow-up data. In the H. pylori -negative cohort, 20 of 102 patients (19.6%) who completed both visits met the same criterion for sustained complete symptom resolution. One of these 24 patients (4.2%) received rescue PPI therapy at month 2 but still met the operational definition, with complete symptom resolution (Likert 1) at both months 6 and 12. The difference between cohorts was not statistically significant (25.5% vs. 19.6%; p = 0.32). After excluding the 24 patients who met the study’s operational definition of sustained complete symptom resolution after successful eradication (nine EPS, eight PDS, and seven overlap), 220 patients remained. Baseline H. pylori positivity was 70.0% in EPS, 32.7% in PDS, and 42.3% in overlap (overall p < 0.001). The adjusted association persisted for EPS versus PDS (aOR, 5.00; 95% CI, 2.56–9.79; p < 0.001) and overlap (aOR, 3.31; 95% CI, 1.55–7.07; p = 0.002).

4. Discussion In our study, we evaluated the distribution of H. pylori infection across functional dyspepsia subgroups in patients diagnosed according to the Rome IV criteria and symptomatic response rates following eradication therapy. The main finding of our study was that H. pylori infection was unevenly distributed across the Rome IV functional dyspepsia subgroups, with the prevalence of infection being significantly higher in the EPS group than in the PDS and PDS–EPS overlap groups. In contrast, PDS was the most common functional dyspepsia subgroup in the overall patient population and among H. pylori -negative patients. Symptomatic response increased over time in both cohorts, and neither the primary nor the LOCF analysis demonstrated a statistically significant between-group difference. Although the conservative sensitivity analysis showed a lower month 12 response in the H. pylori -positive cohort, this difference was not maintained under LOCF, highlighting the influence of missing-data assumptions. Together, these findings support an association between H. pylori infection and the EPS phenotype but do not demonstrate a clear long-term symptomatic advantage following eradication over the H. pylori -negative cohort; differences between cohorts limit causal interpretation.

Functional dyspepsia is one of the common gastrointestinal disorders and has a substantial impact on quality of life and healthcare utilization. A recent comprehensive systematic review and meta-analysis reported a global prevalence of functional dyspepsia of 8.4%, which decreased to 6.8% when the more stringent Rome IV diagnostic criteria were applied [ 10 ]. The application of the Rome IV criteria aims to define functional dyspepsia subgroups based on more specific symptom characteristics and thereby establish more homogeneous patient groups. In our study, of the 425 patients evaluated for dyspeptic symptoms and who underwent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, 244 fulfilled the Rome IV criteria and were classified as having functional dyspepsia. Among patients diagnosed with functional dyspepsia, 43.4% were classified as PDS, 32.4% as EPS, and 24.2% as PDS–EPS overlap. Population-based studies using the Rome IV criteria have reported PDS as the most common functional dyspepsia subgroup, and the predominance of PDS in our study is generally consistent with these findings [ 11 ]. Similarly, the relatively young mean age and the predominance of female patients in our functional dyspepsia cohort are consistent with the literature. However, because our study was not a population-based prevalence study and included symptomatic patients undergoing upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, direct comparison of the distribution of functional dyspepsia and its subgroups in our patient population with population-based prevalence data may not be appropriate [ 12 ].

One of the notable findings of our study was that H. pylori infection was unevenly distributed across the Rome IV functional dyspepsia subgroups, with the prevalence of infection being significantly higher in the EPS group (73.4%) than in the PDS (37.7%) and PDS–EPS overlap (49.2%) groups. The lower overall H. pylori prevalence in our cohort (52.0%) compared with previous reports from Türkiye (65–82.5%) may reflect the exclusion of peptic ulcer disease and recent eradication therapy, together with regional and temporal differences between study populations [ 8 , 9 ]. However, the available evidence regarding the association between H. pylori infection and functional dyspepsia subgroups is limited and not entirely consistent. A study using the Rome III criteria reported that H. pylori infection may influence the pathophysiological characteristics of functional dyspepsia [ 13 ], whereas another study showed that symptomatic benefit following successful eradication was more pronounced particularly in patients with EPS [ 14 ]. These findings support a potential pathophysiological association between H. pylori infection and the EPS subgroup in patients with functional dyspepsia. In contrast, some studies have suggested that the presence of H. pylori does not reliably distinguish between the EPS and PDS subgroups and that symptom-based subgroup classification may be insufficient to predict the pathogenetic role of the infection [ 15 ].

The significant association between EPS and H. pylori observed in our study suggests that chronic gastric inflammation related to the infection may contribute to the development of a pain- and burning-predominant phenotype. The finding that H. pylori -positive patients with functional dyspepsia have a lower gastric sensory threshold and higher levels of sensory neuropeptides suggests a potential link between the infection and visceral hypersensitivity [ 16 ]. However, the high prevalence of H. pylori infection among asymptomatic individuals and the potentially multifactorial pathophysiology of functional dyspepsia preclude interpreting the association observed in our study as evidence of causality. Our findings indicate that, particularly in populations with a high prevalence of H. pylori , the association between the EPS phenotype and infection should be further investigated in larger, multicenter studies using the Rome IV criteria.

In the primary analysis based on patients who achieved successful eradication, no statistically significant differences in symptomatic response rates were observed between the H. pylori -positive and H. pylori -negative cohorts at month 2, month 6, or month 12. However, in the sensitivity analysis that included all patients in the baseline H. pylori -positive and H. pylori -negative cohorts and conservatively classified patients without follow-up data as non-responders, the findings remained unchanged at month 2 and month 6, whereas at month 12, the symptomatic response rate was significantly higher in the H. pylori -negative cohort (68.4% vs. 55.1%; p = 0.034). Most patients lost after month 6 had previously responded (10/12 in the successful-eradication cohort and 6/10 in the negative cohort), and missing responses were more frequent in the baseline positive cohort (29/127 vs. 15/117). The month 12 difference was no longer statistically significant under LOCF, suggesting that the conservative result may partly reflect unequal follow-up loss rather than a difference in symptomatic outcomes.

Nevertheless, our results showed that symptomatic response rates increased over time among H. pylori -positive patients who achieved successful eradication. A similar increase in symptomatic improvement over time was observed in the H. pylori -negative group, and no statistically significant differences in symptomatic response rates were found between the two groups at month 2, month 6, or month 12. This finding suggests that symptomatic improvement in functional dyspepsia is not attributable solely to H. pylori eradication and supports the multifactorial nature of the disorder. Current guidelines and meta-analyses indicate that eradication therapy provides symptomatic benefit in H. pylori -positive patients with functional dyspepsia, although the absolute magnitude of this benefit is limited. In the meta-analysis by Ford et al., eradication therapy significantly improved long-term symptoms compared with placebo, although the magnitude of the symptomatic benefit was reported to be modest [ 5 ]. Similarly, Kang et al. reported symptomatic benefit from eradication in both high (≥50%; RR = 1.17, 95% CI: 1.06–1.29) and low (<50%; RR = 1.21, 95% CI: 1.02–1.44) H. pylori prevalence regions, whereas the Asian subgroup did not reach statistical significance (RR = 1.14, 95% CI: 0.99–1.33) [ 6 ]. These findings suggest that functional dyspepsia cannot be explained by a single pathophysiological mechanism and that multiple factors may contribute to changes in symptoms over time. Functional dyspepsia is currently regarded as a heterogeneous disorder involving the combined effects of impaired gastric motility, visceral hypersensitivity, low-grade duodenal inflammation, impaired mucosal barrier integrity, alterations in the gastrointestinal microbiota, and dysregulation of gut–brain interactions. Therefore, H. pylori infection may represent only one of several factors contributing to symptom development in a specific subgroup of patients [ 1 ]. The similar improvement rates observed among H. pylori -negative patients in our study may likewise reflect the combined effects of these different mechanisms together with the natural course of functional dyspepsia.

Another important aspect of our study is the evaluation of the association between H. pylori and Rome IV functional dyspepsia subgroups and the potential contribution of our findings to the ongoing terminological discussion. According to the Rome IV criteria, H. pylori -positive patients whose symptoms completely resolve for at least six months following successful eradication are considered to have “ H. pylori -associated dyspepsia,” whereas those with persistent symptoms are considered to have functional dyspepsia [ 17 , 18 ]. However, distinguishing between these two clinical entities may not always be straightforward in populations with a high prevalence of H. pylori . In our study, although H. pylori infection was markedly more frequent in the EPS subgroup, symptomatic response following eradication did not differ significantly from that observed in H. pylori -negative patients, suggesting that the presence of H. pylori does not represent a common pathogenetic mechanism in all cases of functional dyspepsia. Nevertheless, the strong association observed with the EPS phenotype may be regarded as a hypothesis-generating finding suggesting that H. pylori infection may play a more prominent role in a specific biological subtype of functional dyspepsia. Sustained complete symptom resolution occurred in 25.5% of evaluable patients following successful eradication and 19.6% of H. pylori -negative patients, without a statistically significant difference. Its occurrence in both cohorts limits attribution of sustained resolution to eradication alone.

From the Rome V perspective, the concept of “disorders of gut–brain interaction” has increasingly been approached through a more precise and mechanism-based framework, with greater emphasis on phenotyping these disorders not only according to symptoms but also according to underlying pathophysiological mechanisms and biological markers [ 19 ]. In this context, our findings provide hypothesis-generating data that may contribute to future mechanism-based phenotyping approaches in functional dyspepsia, integrating biological markers such as H. pylori alongside symptom-based subgroups [ 20 ]. A study investigating a faecal microRNA marker in H. pylori gastritis suggests a potential avenue for further research. Whether such markers can distinguish FD phenotypes or predict symptomatic response requires further investigation [ 21 ]. Additionally, Rome V revises the subgroup definitions, including a lower symptom-frequency threshold for PDS and greater emphasis on the relationship of symptoms to meals. Our cohort was classified using Rome IV; therefore, the observed phenotype distributions should not be directly extrapolated to Rome V [ 22 ].

Our study also has several important strengths. To our knowledge, it is among the first studies conducted in a region with a high prevalence of H. pylori to evaluate both the distribution of H. pylori across functional dyspepsia subgroups classified according to the Rome IV criteria and long-term symptomatic response following eradication. The exclusion of organic pathology in all patients by upper gastrointestinal endoscopy and histopathological examination, the use of a standardized eradication regimen, and follow-up for up to 12 months strengthen the methodological robustness of our study. Furthermore, evaluating not only the presence of H. pylori infection but also its association with Rome IV subgroups provides original data that may contribute to a better understanding of the biological phenotypes of functional dyspepsia.

Our study has several limitations. First, as a single-center observational study, the generalizability of our findings may be limited. In addition, symptom assessment was based on a patient-reported Likert scale, which may be subject to subjective reporting bias. Nevertheless, given that the primary aim of our study was to evaluate the distribution of H. pylori infection across functional dyspepsia subgroups and symptomatic response following eradication, our findings should be confirmed in larger, multicenter prospective studies. Although the primary analysis based on patients who achieved successful eradication was susceptible to selection bias and bias related to loss to follow-up, a conservative sensitivity analysis including the entire baseline cohorts was performed to assess the potential impact of these sources of bias.

Another limitation of our study is that heartburn was distinguished from epigastric burning based on symptom location and the presence of regurgitation. Because these symptoms may overlap in clinical practice, excluding patients with predominant heartburn and/or regurgitation may have introduced some degree of selection or classification bias, particularly in the EPS subgroup, in which epigastric burning is a defining symptom. This should be considered when interpreting the observed association between EPS and H. pylori infection. In addition, three patients in the final cohort had Los Angeles grade A esophagitis, indicating that some overlap between mild reflux findings and functional dyspepsia could not be completely excluded. Finally, reflux symptoms were not assessed using a standardized symptom scale or ambulatory reflux monitoring, which may have limited the accuracy of this distinction.

Another limitation of our study is that H. pylori status was determined solely by histopathological examination and was not confirmed using a second diagnostic method. Although recommended washout periods for PPIs, antibiotics, and bismuth were applied before endoscopy and biopsies were obtained from both the antrum and corpus, the use of histology alone cannot completely exclude the possibility of false-negative results in patients with low bacterial density. Such misclassification could result in truly H. pylori -positive patients being included in the negative group, potentially reducing the observed differences between the groups. However, if the extent of misclassification differed across functional dyspepsia subgroups, the direction of the resulting bias would be difficult to predict.

Because the two cohorts had different treatment exposures at baseline and during follow-up, the comparison of symptomatic response should not be interpreted as an analysis of the isolated effect of H. pylori eradication. Specifically, H. pylori -positive patients with PDS did not receive prokinetics, whereas H. pylori -negative patients with PDS received prokinetic therapy, which may have influenced symptomatic outcomes. Rather, our findings should be interpreted as a comparison of the long-term symptomatic course of two prospectively followed observational cohorts managed differently according to their clinical needs. In addition, although no statistically significant between-group differences were observed in the secondary analysis, the power assessment and the width of the 95% confidence intervals indicate that smaller but clinically meaningful differences cannot be excluded. Therefore, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence in symptomatic response between the two cohorts.

In our study, patients with a diagnosis of anxiety or depression were excluded, and smoking and alcohol use were assessed. However, psychological status was not systematically evaluated using validated scales, and other potential confounding variables, such as socioeconomic status, were not recorded. Therefore, the potential effects of unmeasured confounders, particularly subclinical anxiety and depressive symptoms, on functional dyspepsia subgroup distribution and symptomatic response cannot be completely excluded. Although the longitudinal symptomatic response model was adjusted for baseline FD phenotype, residual confounding from other measured and unmeasured factors cannot be excluded.

5. Conclusions In conclusion, H. pylori infection is not uniformly distributed across Rome IV functional dyspepsia subgroups and is significantly more prevalent in the EPS subgroup. Despite first-line eradication rates of 96.4% per protocol and 83.5% by intention to treat, a clear symptomatic advantage over H. pylori -negative patients was not demonstrated. Differences between the cohorts and incomplete follow-up limit this comparison and do not establish equivalence. Sustained complete symptom resolution occurred in 25.5% of evaluable patients after successful eradication and 19.6% of H. pylori -negative patients, limiting attribution to eradication alone. Our findings support the possibility that H. pylori infection may play a more prominent role in specific biological subtypes of functional dyspepsia and provide hypothesis-generating data that may contribute to the mechanism-based phenotyping approach envisioned in the Rome V framework. Large-scale, multicenter prospective studies involving patient populations from different geographical regions are needed to confirm these findings.

Background In dyspeptic patients without alarm symptoms, the “Test-and-Treat” (TT) strategy aims to alleviate symptoms and prevent adverse outcomes. An alternative workup expands the TT-strategy by incorporating esophagogastroduodenoscopy (Test-Treat-and-Scope [TT-S]).

Objective This prospective cross-sectional study provides evidence-based insights into the clinical workup of dyspepsia by applying the TT and TT-S options. Design In a consecutive cohort of 2171 dyspeptic patients without alarm symptoms, H. pylori (Hp) status was assessed by 13 C-Urea Breath Test, Rapid urease test, and histology. Histology profiling was based on six biopsies and included atrophy staging (OLGA-system).

Results Among Hp -positive and Hp -negative patients, the prevalence of mucosal atrophy was 22.2% and 1.3% ( p < 0.001), respectively. In the study population, 92.5% did not exhibit atrophic disease (OLGA stage 0). Among Hp -positive patients, mucosal atrophy occurred in 142/640 subjects. Nine in 640 (1.4%) Hp -positive patients presented advanced atrophy (OLGA-stages III-IV), considered at high-risk for gastric cancer. The overall prevalence of high-risk OLGA stages (III-IV) was below 1.5% (all Hp -positive). The mean age of patients with OLGA stages III-IV was 15 years older than that of non-atrophic patients ( p < 0.0001). In all atrophic OLGA-stages, Hp- positive subjects dominated over the Hp -negative (test-for-trend; p < 0.0001). None of the Hp -negative subjects showed extensive atrophy (OLGA-stages III-IV).

Conclusion In the considered epidemiological context, advanced gastric atrophy (OLGA-stages III-IV), consistently recognized as at risk of cancer development, only occurred in Hp- positive patients over 55 years. These results support the priority of the TT-S-strategy in Hp -positive patients older than 55, even in the absence of alarm symptoms.
