Among general and endoscopy populations, the prevalence of dyspepsia varies according to its clinical definitions [ 1 , 2 ]. Organic dyspepsia coexists with endoscopically/histologically detectable anatomic lesions, including inflammatory diseases, erosions/ulcers, early and advanced pre-malignant, and malignant diseases. Functional dyspepsia refers to a symptomatic condition without identifiable organic disease [ 3 , 4 ]. The prevalence of functional versus organic dyspepsia is biased by the subjective perception of symptoms and the epidemiological prevalence of organic etiologies. The clinical profile of dyspeptic patients with no alarm symptoms (e.g., family history of gastric cancer, unintentional weight loss, hematemesis, progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, recurrent vomiting, and laboratory signs of gastrointestinal bleeding) does not significantly differ in functional and organic cases. However, this distinction has a significant impact on patient management, affecting both therapeutic choices and patient follow-up [ 5 ].

Helicobacter pylori ( H. pylori ) infection causes chronic, non-self-limiting inflammation and atrophy of the gastric mucosa, impaired stomach function, gastric dysbiosis, and a genotoxic microenvironment. The bacterial infection, especially its more virulent strains, is a known cause of dyspepsia and the leading cause of sporadic gastric cancer (GC) [ 6 – 9 ]. In H. pylori -positive patients with dyspepsia, bacterial eradication can successfully treat gastric symptoms and reduce the risk of inflammation-associated GC.

In populations with a high prevalence of H. pylori infection, the ‘Test and Treat’ (TT) strategy aims to alleviate symptoms and prevent adverse outcomes associated with the disease. In line with its primary aim, this ‘basic’ workup excludes additional diagnostic procedures, thereby expanding the population that can benefit from immediate bacterial eradication. One disadvantage of the ‘test and treat’ strategy is that it fails to detect gastric precancerous or cancerous lesions in H. pylori -infected patients whose symptoms resolve following eradication therapy [ 10 – 29 ].

An alternative clinical workup of H. pylori -associated dyspepsia expands the Test-and-Treat strategy by adding esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). This combination of non-invasive and invasive procedures (Test-Treat-and-Scope [TT-S]) enhances diagnostic accuracy, enabling the detection of precancerous lesions that significantly impact patient management [ 30 – 32 ]. Furthermore, this approach allows for the collection of biological samples to test for antibiotic resistance and prevent the use of ineffective medical treatments. Limited access to endoscopy and biopsy procedures, as well as their associated costs, may pose a significant challenge to the routine implementation of the Test-Treat and Scope approach [ 10 – 26 , 28 , 29 ].

Adjunctive factors supporting the choice of the dyspepsia workup include the epidemiological context (e.g., the country’s demographics, H. pylori prevalence and virulence, and the country-specific gastric cancer risk), the healthcare system (e.g., whether it is public or private and the investment in cancer screening programs), the country’s gross domestic product, and patients’ expectancies. All such variables may affect both the Guidelines and the experts’ recommendations [ 33 – 37 ]. In a consecutive cohort of 2171 dyspeptic patients with no alarm symptoms, this study aims to provide evidence-based information on the clinical management of dyspepsia by applying the TT and TT-S options.

Patients & methods Epidemiological setting of the study and criteria for patient enrollment This prospective cross-sectional cohort study was conducted in an Italian region (Emilia-Romagna), where the prevalence of H. pylori infection in the endoscopy population ranges from 25 to 35% in urban and suburban areas. In 2018, there were 795 deaths due to gastric cancer in this region, accounting for 1.6% of all deaths and 5.6% of cancer-related deaths. Between January 2022 and August 2024, 2213 consecutive patients were referred by their physician to the Digestive Endoscopy Unit (IRCCS Azienda Ospedaliero-Universitaria di Bologna) for dyspepsia with no alarm symptoms.

From the original consecutive cohort of 2213 subjects, the following 42 individuals were excluded based on the following criteria: Age younger than 18 or older than 90 years (4 patients); Presence of alarm symptoms (family history of GC, unintentional weight loss, hematemesis, progressive dysphagia or odynophagia, recurrent vomiting, and laboratory signs of gastrointestinal bleeding) (2 patients); Antisecretory therapies and/or antibiotics within the previous 2 weeks since esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (EGD) (8 patients); Previous H. pylori successful eradication (6 patients); Previous gastric surgery or endoscopic mucosal resection/dissection (2 patients);

Biopsy sampling protocol inconsistent with the gastritis staging (two biopsy specimens from the antral mucosa, one from the angularis incisura, and two from oxyntic mucosa: 2 patients); Serological testing indicating celiac disease or gastric autoimmune diseases (e.g., positive anti-parietal cell or intrinsic factor antibodies, elevated gastrin, low vitamin B12) (5 patients); Declined to participate in the study (13 patients). Esophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (EGD) After initial testing for H. pylori infection (13 C-urea breath test; see below), all patients underwent EGD (Olympus→ GIF-100 gastroscope; Japan) regardless of their H. pylori status.
An experienced gastroenterologist (DV) performed the endoscopy and biopsy sampling (submitted by the gastric compartment).

The endoscopy features were categorized based on the dominant findings (no focal lesions versus erosions or ulcers, either active or healed scars). The location of erosions or ulcers was also recorded, distinguishing between duodenal and distal gastric mucosa down to the incisura angularis from proximal lesions. Six biopsy samples were collected from each patient: two from the distal mucous-secreting gastric antrum, two from the antral-oxyntic border at the incisura angularis , and two from the gastric oxyntic corpus/ fundus mucosa. The tissue specimens were placed in two vials, distinguishing antral/angular from oxyntic biopsy samples. Two additional biopsy samples were obtained from the gastric antrum for rapid urease test.

13 C-urea breath test (UBT) 13 C-urea breath test (UBT) used the Expirobacter kit from Sofar Alfasigma S.p.A in Bologna, Italy, according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A test was considered positive if DOB was at least 5‰. Rapid urease test (RUT) Rapid urease test ([RUT], UFT-300 kit Healthcare S.r.l., Milan, Italy). The tissue specimen was immersed in a liquid containing red phenol and urea. The change in the liquid’s color (from yellow to magenta) indicated a positive result.

Pathology Biopsy specimens were fixed in formalin (5% dilution) and embedded in paraffin. Hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining was performed on 4 to 6-micron-thick histological sections. The H. pylori status was histologically assessed using a modified Giemsa stain; immunohistochemistry for H. pylori was applied when necessary. Two experienced pathologists (AD, LT) jointly evaluated the biopsy sets based on internationally validated criteria. The histological assessment always included the OLGA staging system, which combines the atrophy scores assessed in the antral and oxyntic stomach compartments [ 38 – 41 ]. Figure 1 summarizes the criteria for OLGA staging as proposed in its original publication.

Fig. 1 OLGA (Operative Link on Gastritis Assessment) Staging System for gastric mucosa atrophy. The combination of the score values obtained from the two gastric compartments results in the atrophy stage. Score values for atrophy to be applied in mucous-secreting/antral (including angulus ) and oxyntic/corpus-fundus mucosa: Score 0 = no atrophy in the specimens obtained from the same compartment; Score 1 : atrophy (non-metaplastic and metaplastic) involving 1–30% of the specimens obtained from the same compartment; Score 2 : atrophy (non-metaplastic and metaplastic) involving 30–60% of the specimens obtained from the same compartment; Score 3 : atrophy (non-metaplastic and metaplastic) involving > 60% of the specimens obtained from the same compartment. The stages considered high-risk for gastric cancer are highlighted in bold

Assessment of the H. pylori status In all patients, H. pylori status was assessed by three methods: (a) 13 C-Urea Breath Test (UBT), (b) Rapid urease test (RUT), (c) histology. H. pylori -positive status was based on histology and either a positive UBT or RUT. In discordant results, at least two concordant tests were required to confirm the patient’s infection with H. pylori .

Ethical approval The study was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the local Ethics Committee (Protocol No. 47/2012/OSS). Before enrolment, all participants gave written informed consent. Patients or the public were not involved in the design, or conduct, or reporting, or dissemination plans of our research.

Statistics The Cochran-Armitage Test was used to identify trends among the proportion of H. pylori -positive patients and subjects older than 55 over the different OLGA stages. The Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric test compared the mean age among OLGA stages. To compare the associations of OLGA stage II versus stages 0-I with H. pylori status, Odds Ratios (OR) were calculated by fitting a multivariable logistic regression model to the data, adjusting for sex, age classes, nationality, and smoking. This calculation excluded seven patients with OLGA stage III and two with OLGA stage IV because they all tested positive for H. pylori status, leading to model convergence failure. The SAS EG v.7.15 (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA) statistical package was used for all analyses. All statistical tests were two-tailed. A p -value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Results Figure 2 presents the study population of 2171 individuals, by their H. pylori status and histological mucosa phenotyping. The overall prevalence of bacterial infection was 29.5%. Among H. pylori -positive and H. pylori -negative patients, the prevalence of gastric mucosal atrophy was 22.2% and 1.3% ( p < 0.001), respectively. Fig. 2 Study population by H. pylori status and gastric mucosa histology phenotyping at the enrollment

Study population: demographics, Helicobacter pylori status, endoscopy, and histological findings Table 1 displays demographics, smoking habits, and the endoscopy and histological phenotype of all 2171 individuals by age groups (< 55 versus ≥ 55) and H. pylori status.

The patient cohort included 577 males and 1394 females (M: F = 0.58), with no sex prevalence by H. pylori status ( p = 0.07). The prevalence of H. pylori -negative dyspeptic subjects (70.5%) was higher than that of H. pylori -positive patients (25.5%). H. pylori -negative subjects significantly prevailed in the Italian native population ( p = 0.0001). No significant difference emerged between H. pylori status and smoking habits ( p = 0.45).

All erosions/ulcers were found in the H. pylori -positive group (overall prevalence 42/640: 10/640 in the pre-pyloric/duodenal areas, and 32/640 in the proximal stomach, including the mucus-secreting oxyntic border along the lesser curvature). Only one H. pylori -negative patient had focal lesions (erosion). Among H. pylori -positive individuals, erosive/ulcer lesions were significantly linked to age over 55 ( p < 0.0001). In the study population, 2009 out of 2171 subjects (92.5%) did not show atrophic disease (OLGA stage 0).

Among H. pylori -positive patients, histological phenotyping of the gastric mucosa documented mucosal atrophy in 142 out of 640 subjects. Atrophic lesions only involved the antral mucosa in 106 subjects (74.6%). In 36/142 (25.3%) patients, low-grade (i.e.: G1) atrophic lesions were also documented in oxyntic specimens. The combination of antral and oxyntic atrophy scores resulted in 9/640 (1.4%) H. pylori -positive patients harboring high-risk OLGA stages (stage III-IV).

Among H. pylori -negative patients, 20/1531 (1.3%) featured mucosal atrophy. Low-grade (i.e.: G1) atrophic lesions always involved the antral compartment; in 4/20 patients, low-grade (i.e.: G1) atrophy also involved oxyntic mucosa.

The overall prevalence of high-risk gastritis stages (OLGA stages III-IV = 9/640) was below 1.5% and all these clustered in the H. pylori positive group. The mean age of patients with high-risk gastritis stages (OLGA stages III-IV) was more than 15 years older than that of patients without atrophic lesions ( p < 0.0001). In all atrophic OLGA stages (I-II-III-IV), H. pylori- positive subjects dominated over the H. pylori -negative subjects (stage I = 83.9%; stage II = 97.1%; stages III and IV = 100%) (test for trend; p < 0.0001). None of the H. pylori -negative subjects showed high-risk OLGA stages (stage III-IV).

Risk factors for high-risk gastritis stages Using the mean age of the population (55 years), a significant correlation was found between increasing age and increased values of the atrophy stages (OLGA 0 = 25%; OLGA I = 75%; OLGA II = 86%; OLGA III = 100%; OLGA IV = 100%; Cochran-Armitage Trend Test: p < 0.0001). Univariate analysis evaluated the risk of having high-stage OLGA (i.e., OLGA stages III-IV, considered high-risk for GC) based on sex, age, country of birth, smoking habits, and H. pylori status. A significantly increased risk emerged only for increasing age (as a continuous variable; OR = 1.084; 95% CI 1.024–1.160). There was no significant increased risk associated with sex (OR = 1.438; 95% CI 0.355–5.447) or country of birth (OR = 0.779; 95% CI 0.042–4.267). Based on the evidence that all nine cases of advanced atrophic gastritis (OLGA stage III and IV) occurred in H. pylori -positive patients, these cases were excluded from a second analysis focusing on the association between H. pylori infection and the risk of developing stage II atrophy, the most advanced stage among the low-risk stages (OLGA 0–II). A multivariable logistic regression model - adjusted for sex, age (as a continuous variable), smoking status, and country of birth - showed a significantly higher risk of OLGA stage II among H. pylori -positive patients compared to those with stage 0 or I (OR = 95.2; 95% CI 20.350 to > 999.999) (Table 2 ). The model also indicated that each additional year of age increased the risk of OLGA progression by approximately 7% (OR = 1.07; 95% CI 1.038–1.107). Given the strong influence of both H. pylori positive status and advancing age on progression to stage II, a second logistic model was used to estimate the impact of age as a categorical variable (< 55 versus ≥ 55 years). The model predicted a probability of 8.5% for OLGA stage II in patients aged 55 or older, compared with 1.7% in younger patients.

Discussion In real-world clinical practice, dyspepsia ranks among the most common indications for endoscopy/biopsy procedures [ 42 , 43 ]. The subjective perception of symptoms and the variable proportion of functional or organic dyspepsia etiology challenge the choice of its clinical work-up [ 44 , 45 ].

H. pylori is a leading cause of dyspepsia [ 46 ]. The prevalence of bacterial infection, its virulence, and associated gastric and extra-gastric lesions vary significantly by epidemiological context [ 47 – 50 ]. In countries where H. pylori -associated dyspepsia is common and access to endoscopy is limited, the test-and-treat approach aims to identify and eliminate the causative agent, ultimately reducing gastric cancer risk [ 51 , 52 ]. In regions with low H. pylori prevalence, the small number of dyspeptic patients testing positive for H. pylori could benefit from an endoscopy approach that involves detecting at-risk lesions. This choice also allows for collecting samples to tailor antibiotic treatment accordingly [ 53 ].

These approaches differ significantly in method, cost, clinical yield, and applicability in different epidemiological and healthcare contexts [ 54 ]. In Asian countries with a high prevalence of H. pylori- related gastric cancer, a more “vigilant” strategy is employed [ 55 ]. In a recent meta-analysis including 81 studies from 19 Asian countries, the pooled prevalence of early precancerous gastric lesions was 26.1% (95% CI 22.7–30.0) for chronic atrophic gastritis (CAG) and 22.9% (95%CI 19.7–26.6) for intestinal metaplasia (IM). In the same study, significant odds ratios were found to be associated with H . pylori infection, with both CAG (2.16; 95% CI, 2.09–2.22) and IM (1.64; 95% CI, 1.57–1.72) being statistically significant. Specifically focusing on a pediatric population, a systematic review and meta-analysis by Abdun and coauthors found that among pediatric H. pylori -infected individuals, the overall prevalence of precancerous lesions (i.e., chronic atrophic gastritis with or without IM) was 17.2%. The rates of precancerous lesions in infected individuals were more common in subjects over ten years old and varied significantly across regions, ranging from 33.8% in Africa to 6.3% in Europe. Moreover, in the Chinese pediatric population, more advanced precancerous lesions (i.e., dysplasia) were also identified (1,4%) [ 56 ]. This epidemiological evidence strongly supports the rationale for implementing universal endoscopic screening beginning in middle age (TT-S) in populations with a high prevalence of H. pylori infection, regardless of patients’ symptoms. In Japan, this strategy is part of the national secondary prevention policy for GC. In a similar epidemiological context, South Korea adopts a proactive approach by implementing culture or molecular testing to guide eradication therapy (Table 3 ).

The dyspepsia workup differs significantly in Western countries, with H. pylori prevalence being considerably lower than in Asian countries. North America (USA and Canada) favors a non-invasive approach (e.g., UBT or stool antigen test) in patients under 60 years without alarm features. Upper endoscopy is reserved for older individuals or those with clinical “red flags”. Meanwhile, based on the British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines, the United Kingdom suggests a test-and-treat strategy in dyspeptic patients under 55 years, with endoscopy indicated for those ≥ 55 years or younger individuals presenting with alarm symptoms [ 10 – 29 ].

This variability in health strategies highlights how risk stratification impacts clinical decision-making in managing dyspepsia, depending on the prevalence of cancer-promoting H. pylori infection, resource availability (gross domestic product), public health policies (including population screening programs), and overall population empowerment [ 51 , 57 ]. Table 3 details the international strategies from the past decade regarding TT versus TT-S strategies. When distinguishing between dyspepsia with and without alarm symptoms, the table highlights common recommendations for using the test-and-treat approach for patients who do not show alarm symptoms. The recommended age for the test-and-scope strategy varies significantly, ranging from 35 (Vietnam) to 60 (UK). Except for Thailand, the suggested age reflects each country’s specific incidence rates of gastric cancer (GC). In regions with lower GC incidence, the age cutoff for endoscopy screening is generally older.

The present study, conducted in an epidemiological context with H. pylori prevalence below 30%, has associated the infection with a global prevalence of atrophy of less than one-fourth of the considered endoscopy population. Additionally, none of the 1531 dyspeptic patients (of any age) who tested negative for H. pylori showed high-risk stages of atrophy. This finding further emphasizes the clinical priority of non-invasive testing for H. pylori status in the initial dyspepsia workup.

Univariate and multivariate statistics related to H. pylori positive status and increasing age significantly raise the risk of atrophy. In the considered population, the TT-S strategy using a cutoff of 55 years would detect all patients with advanced gastric histology [ 52 ]. In H. pylori- positive patients, current infection was linked to a stage progression of about 7% per year, providing evidence-based support for timely eradication.

Several factors limit the generalizability of the present results: (a) the country-specific epidemiology of H. pylori infection; (b) the healthcare setting of the study; (c) the pragmatic study design, which does not account for dyspeptic patients who were not referred for endoscopy or who declined the procedure; and (d) the single-center project resulting in endoscopic assessments performed by only one endoscopist. Additionally, there is a lack of information regarding the H. pylori strains in infected patients, which restricts our understanding of how the bacterium’s virulence influences the progression of atrophy. The strengths of this study include recruiting a large cohort of consecutive outpatients from a real-world gastroenterology practice, utilizing a standardized protocol for gastric biopsy sampling, and internationally consistent histological criteria.

In conclusion, this study highlights the clinical significance of testing H. pylori status in the diagnostic approach for patients with dyspepsia. In the considered epidemiological setting, no H. pylori -negative dyspeptic patients without alarm symptoms showed at-risk lesions. The potential occurrence of advanced atrophy in H. pylori -positive patients over 55 years underscores the importance of test-treat and scope, even in subjects without alarm symptoms. ABSTRACT Background Functional dyspepsia (FD) affects over 7% of the global population, impairing quality of life and driving significant healthcare burden. Although genetic contributions to FD pathophysiology have been suspected, large, well‐powered genetic studies remain limited. We aimed to identify FD genetic risk factors and implicated biological pathways.

Methods We performed a FD genome‐wide association study in 1,168,899 European individuals, including 29,584 FD cases from five large biobanks. We dissected the genetic architecture of FD and its overlap with gastrointestinal and psychiatric disorders and conducted comprehensive gene‐prioritization, regulatory, and cell‐type enrichment analyzes to identify pathophysiological mechanisms and actionable targets.

Key Results We show FD is a complex, highly polygenic trait with a significant genetic component (3.63% heritability) but lower than similar gastrointestinal disorders like irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Mendelian randomization revealed causal effects of depression and anxiety on FD risk. We observed substantial local genetic correlations with IBS and GERD, including shared genome‐wide significant signals at the human leukocyte antigen region, supporting immune‐mediated mechanisms. Gene‐prioritization analyzes converged on DEAH‐Box Helicase 36 ( DHX36 ), involved in immune responses to microbial infections. Integrative expression‐quantitative trait loci and colocalization analyzes indicated that higher genetic risk of FD is causally associated with a reduced DHX36 expression in gastrointestinal tissues, potentially triggering increased proinflammatory cytokine production.

Conclusions & Inferences This study implicates immune‐driven pathways in FD susceptibility, adds insights into the pathophysiological mechanisms of the disease, and reveals DHX36 as a candidate target for future investigation. Key Points Functional Dyspepsia (FD) is a highly polygenic trait with a modest but significant heritability, estimated at 3.63% in the European population. We identified substantial local genetic overlap at multiple loci between FD and both IBS and GERD and observed that depression and anxiety exert predisposing causal effects on FD risk.

Genetic variants affecting immune‐related genes (HLA and DHX36 ) are associated with FD through increased gastrointestinal inflammatory responses, supporting an immune‐mediated component and offering candidate targets for further mechanistic investigation.

Plain Language Summary Functional dyspepsia (FD) is a disorder of gut‐brain interaction characterized by symptoms originating in the upper digestive tract, although its underlying causes remain largely unexplained. This study examined genetic data from over 1 million individuals to better understand the biological mechanisms contributing to the condition. FD has a heritable component and shares a substantial proportion of its genetic basis with clinically related gastrointestinal disorders and psychiatric conditions. The strongest genetic evidence pointed toward altered immune and inflammatory responses that may be shared across disorders affecting the upper gastrointestinal tract. Together, these findings highlight the interplay between the gut, brain, and immune system in FD.

Our findings indicate that genetic variants in immune‐related genes ( HLA‐DQB1 and DHX36 ) may influence functional dyspepsia risk by modulating gastrointestinal inflammatory responses, reinforcing the role of an immune‐mediated component in disease susceptibility and nominating these genes for further mechanistic investigation. Besides the cardinal symptoms of postprandial fullness, early satiation, epigastric pain, and epigastric burning, this condition has also been linked with psychological symptoms such as anxiety and depression [ 2 ]. In current clinical practice guidelines, treatment options for FD are limited in efficacy and level of evidence [ 3 ]. The development of novel therapeutic options is hampered by the observed large placebo response in clinical trials (30%–40%), the heterogeneity of this symptom‐based condition, and the associated difficulty in establishing the underlying pathophysiology in individual patients [ 4 ]. It includes alterations in gastric motility such as delayed gastric emptying and impaired gastric accommodation, duodenal alterations such as impaired barrier function, or altered signal transmission toward the brain [ 5 ]. All of these may have specific underlying genetic predisposition through altered neurotransmitter or gut peptide signaling, altered immune function, or altered mucosal integrity [ 6 , 7 ].

A role for genetics in the pathophysiology of FD has been suspected based on twin and family studies [ 8 ], and previous biobank‐scale investigations [ 9 ]. Despite adequate sample size, however, the latter have failed to identify unequivocal risk genes and mechanisms. Here we report a genome‐wide association study (GWAS) meta‐analysis of FD in 29,584 cases and 1,139,315 controls of European ancestry from five population‐based biobanks. With this sample size in hand, we reported on the genetic architecture of FD and its overlap with gastrointestinal (GI) and psychiatric disorders and proposed candidate genes and mechanisms that warrant further investigation.

2 Methods 2.1 Study Cohorts FD was studied in five population‐based cohorts, totalling 1,168,899 European individuals. The phenotype was defined based on different versions of main and/or secondary International Classifications of Diseases (ICD). Genetic data relevant to the Estonian Genomic Centre of the University of Tartu (EGCUT) [ 10 ] and the UK Biobank (UKB) [ 11 ] cohorts were obtained from previously reported FD GWAS summary statistics [ 9 ]. The Michigan Genomics Initiative (MGI) data freeze 3, consisting of 50,000 European individuals, was employed upon approval from the University of Michigan Institutional Review Board. Further, publicly available GWAS from FinnGen (K11_FUNCDYSP, data freeze R10) [ 12 ] using ICD8, ICD9, and ICD10 codes and the Million Veteran Program (MVP; Dyspepsia and other specified disorders of function of stomach) [ 13 ], using the PheCode 536.8 were added to the study.

2.2 GWAS Meta‐Analysis GWAS summary statistics were quality‐checked, lifted‐over to GRCh37, harmonized, and assigned to a valid rsID with the python package GWASlab [ 14 ]. Individual GWAS were integrated using METAL [ 15 ] and only variants present in at least 30% of the total sample size with no heterogeneity in their effect sizes across studies were kept. Finally, GWASinspector [ 16 ] was employed to further remove duplicated or missing variants and mismatched, ambiguous and multi‐allelic variants that could not be verified. 2.3 Heritability, Genetic Correlations and Overlap With Other Traits SNP‐based heritability ( h 2

SNP ) was estimated via linkage disequilibrium score regression (LDSC) [ 17 ] at the liability scale. Pre‐computed linkage disequilibrium (LD) matrices from the 1000G were employed. Batch genetic correlations were carried out to decipher the overall genetic similarity of FD with 2871 publicly available GWAS from the CTG‐VL platform ( https://vl.genoma.io/ ). Only significantly correlated traits after false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment for multiple tests and a significant heritability ( h 2 SNP Z ‐score ≥ 3) were considered.

Local genetic correlations with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), depression disorder (DEP), and anxiety disorder (ANX) were carried out using LAVA [ 18 ] (Table S2 ). First, univariate analysis estimates h 2 SNP for each locus for each trait and, thereafter, bivariate analysis estimates the local covariance for each locus and pair of traits. Pre‐calculated UKB LD references were used. Multiple testing was accounted for using Bonferroni correction. To colocalize loci with significant genetic correlation and GWAS signals, GWAS Catalog [ 19 ] was consulted for GERD, IBS, DEP (“Depression”, “Major depressive disorder”, and “Depressed affect”), and ANX.

2.4 Mendelian Randomization Analyzes Bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR) analyzes were performed to investigate potential causal relationships between FD and highly‐correlated digestive and psychiatric traits using the R package TwoSampleMR [ 20 ] (v0.6.8). Traits relevant to gut motility, such as constipation, diarrhea, and stool frequency (SF) were also included (Table S3 ). Independent instrumental variables strongly associated with the exposure were identified through LD clumping using an r

2 threshold of 0.001, a 10 Mb window, and a suggestive significance threshold ( p < 5 × 10 −6 ). Only variants with F ‐statistic > 10 were retained. The multiplicative random‐effects inverse variance weighted estimator was used as the primary model, with additional estimators applied to account for different assumptions regarding instrumental variable validity. We assessed robustness using Cochran's Q , MR Egger intercept, and Steiger directionality tests. Significant p ‐value thresholds were set at p < 0.001, p < 0.01, and p < 0.05.

2.5 Locus Definition, Gene Mapping and Prioritization Independent genomic risk loci were defined using FUMA [ 21 ] considering SNPs at suggestive significance ( p ≤ 5 × 10 −6 ) not in LD ( r 2 < 0.6). For LD blocks closer than 250 kbp apart, association signals were merged into a single locus. The SNP2GENE pipeline from FUMA was used to map genes positionally (maximum distance of 10 kbp) and through eQTL.

To systematically prioritize genes from our GWAS meta‐analysis, an integrative strategy combining statistical, functional, and causal approaches was employed. Gene‐based association tests were performed using MAGMA [ 22 ] and fastBAT [ 23 ]. A transcriptome‐wide association study (TWAS) across GTEx [ 24 ] tissues relevant to FD (brain and GI) was carried out via S‐MultiXcan [ 25 ]. To assess potential causal relationships between gene expression and the GWAS signals, summary‐based MR (SMR) [ 26 ] was applied using eQTL data from the most significant tissues. In addition, two databases of regulatory elements were inspected to explore how the genetic variants in the prioritized locus may change chromatin accessibility status, overlap with transcription binding sites and alter histone modifications, namely FORGEdb ( https://forgedb.cancer.gov/ ) and RegulomeDB ( https://regulomedb.org/regulome‐search/ ). Finally, genetic interactions with approved or investigational drugs were assessed by querying the DrugBank ( https://go.drugbank.com/ ), Open Targets Platform ( https://platform.opentargets.org/ ), and DGIdb ( https://dgidb.org/ ) databases.

2.6 Tissue and Cell Type Prioritization Different gene‐level enrichment analysis approaches were performed to identify tissues and cell types potentially relevant to FD. First, MAGMA gene‐property analysis was conducted using GTEx gene expression data to identify enrichment of gene‐level associations in tissue‐specific expression profiles. Subsequently, these gene‐level associations were employed to test cell type specificity of FD as part of FUMA Cell Type analysis [ 27 ]. Similarly, DEPICT [ 28 ] was used to identify tissue and/or cell types in which associated genes were differentially expressed. Finally, stratified LDSC [ 29 ] was applied to identify tissues where genetic variants disproportionately contribute to trait heritability.

2.7 FD —Gastroparesis ( GP ) Genetic Overlap Publicly available GP GWAS were obtained from GWAS Catalog, under the accession numbers GCST90295922 [ 30 ] and GCST90478363 [ 13 ], and used for fixed‐effects meta‐analysis using METAL, as described above. SNP‐based heritability was calculated on the liability scale using different estimations of the GP population prevalence (0.02%–2.0%), based on epidemiological studies [ 30 , 31 , 32 ]. Genetic correlation with FD was assessed using LDSC, as described above.

3 Results 3.1 Characteristics of the Cohorts FD was investigated across five population‐based cohorts, comprising a total of 29,584 cases and 1,139,315 controls of European ancestry (Table S1 ). Across the population‐based cohorts, the prevalence of FD was generally consistent, averaging 2.6% ± 0.6%. An exception was observed in the EGCUT biobank, which consisted of a nested case–control dataset, not the entire population, resulting in a higher case‐to‐total‐sample‐size proportion of 0.128 (12.8%). Female participants outnumbered males in all cohorts (53.1%–65.2%), with the sole exception of the MVP biobank, where women comprised only 7.5% of the sample. Participant ages varied between cohorts, ranging from an average of 42 years in EGCUT to 64 years in MVP.

3.2 FD GWAS Meta‐Analysis: Heritability, Genetic Correlations and Overlap With Other Traits A GWAS meta‐analysis of FD resulted in 9,638,985 high‐quality genetic variants with no signs of population stratification (LDSC intercept = 1.02). Based on LDSC analysis, a limited but significant SNP heritability (see Section 2 ) was estimated at 3.63%. FD correlated with 724 traits and anti‐correlated with 108 traits ( p FDR < 0.05; h 2 SNP

Z ‐score ≥ 3) (Table S4 ). Traits belonging to the digestive domain were among those with the highest genetic correlation estimates ( r g ), including disorders which commonly overlap in FD, such as IBS or GERD [ 33 ], treatments or medication used to alleviate these, and both extremes of the SF spectrum: constipation and diarrhea (Figure 1 ). Similarly, anxiety/panic attacks were highly correlated with FD as well as depression and known medications to treat these psychiatric disorders. A wide variety of pain‐related traits, besides the expected abdominal pain, were also found among the top correlated traits. Interestingly, disorders from the musculoskeletal domain and inflammatory‐driven disorders (chronic pharyngitis, respiratory diseases, inflammatory diseases of the prostate) were also found among the top correlated traits, highlighting a plausible shared pathophysiological mechanism with FD.

We performed a more detailed analysis of the genetic overlap of FD with two GI disorders, IBS and GERD, and two psychiatric disorders, DEP and ANX (Table S2 ). Bonferroni < 0.05), albeit none of them was in common with IBS (five loci) or DEP (two loci). About half of the loci showing genetic correlation with GERD or IBS colocalized with GWAS signals from any of the traits examined. In particular, locus 961 (human leukocyte antigen region; HLA) and locus 1719 ( NCAM1 locus) were characterized by the presence of common GWAS signals to all traits under study, highlighting potential underlying pleiotropic effects (Table S5 ).

To assess possible causative links between FD and highly correlated traits from the digestive and psychiatric domain, bidirectional MR analyzes were carried out (Figure 2 ; Table S6 ). We found bidirectional causative effects of FD with IBS, GERD, and diaphragmatic hernia, pointing to potential reciprocal effects or shared pathways (Figure 2A ). Further, directional pleiotropy may also explain the relationships observed with IBS and GERD as evidenced by the different sensitivity methods analyzed (Table S6 ). Similar findings were obtained for constipation, whereas diarrhea and SF showed no convincing evidence of association (Figure 2B ). Finally, our MR analyzes strongly supported a causal effect of anxiety and depression on FD (Figure 2C ). All estimators yielded significant positive effects (Odds Ratio, OR > 1; p < 0.05) with no evidence of horizontal pleiotropy, heterogeneity, or outliers (Table S6 ).

3.3 Annotation of FD Genomic Risk Loci A single genome‐wide significant ( p < 5 × 10 −8 ) locus was detected, located in the HLA region (Table 1 ; Figure S2 ). The SNPs in this locus positionally mapped to 137 genes and through expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) to 155 genes. Specifically, the leadSNP (rs9274481; 6:32633756:C:T) fell in the HLA Class II region and physically mapped to the HLA‐DQB1 as the nearest gene. Querying GWAS ATLAS ( https://atlas.ctglab.nl/PheWAS ) and IEU OpenGWAS [ 34 ] repositories revealed that this variant has been previously associated with an increased risk of autoimmune diseases like coeliac disease, Type 1 diabetes, or inflammatory bowel disease (Table S7 ). Of note, the reported associations have been mostly discovered in genetic studies based on the FinnGen cohort. In line with that observation, FinnGen was the major contributor to the signal detected in the FD GWAS meta‐analysis (Figure S3 ), albeit the direction of effects among the suggestive significant SNPs in the locus remained consistent across the individual cohorts (Figure S4 ). Twenty‐nine additional association signals were detected at a suggestive level of significance (Table 1 ). Sixty unique protein coding genes positionally and/or eQTL mapped to these loci after excluding those mapped to the two loci located at the HLA region (locus 16 and 17).

3.4 Gene Prioritization Analysis An in‐depth functional characterization of the FD associated genetic variants was performed applying different methodologies and data sources to assess gene‐level associations, functional relevance, and regulatory mechanisms (see Section 2 ). We used gene‐based association tests (MAGMA and fastBAT) that combine genetic signals within the same gene, highlighting 642 genes associated at nominal significance ( p < 0.05) (Tables S8 and S9 ). We also examined whether changes in gene activity in relevant tissues, particularly the brain and gastrointestinal tract, might play a role, using a TWAS approach based on GTEx data (see Section 2 ). This approach revealed a single gene‐tissue signature that passed FDR correction ( p

FDR < 0.05), consisting of a reduced expression of DEAH‐Box Helicase 36 ( DHX36 ) in GI tissues (Table S10 ). To explore whether these gene‐expression changes might be driving the genetic associations we observed, we applied the SMR method to the tissues showing the strongest evidence. Following this method, we causally linked specific genetic variants associated with a higher risk of FD and a reduced expression of DHX36 (Table S11 ; Figure 3 ). Several of these genetic variants overlap with transcription factor binding motifs, chromatin accessibility hotspots and other regulatory elements, providing plausible mechanisms underlying DHX36 altered expression (Figure 3 ). Across all prioritization strategies, only two genes, DHX36 and Rho Guanine Nucleotide Exchange Factor 26 ( ARHGEF26 ), were consistently highlighted (Figure 4 ). Finally, we looked for potential links between these genes and existing or experimental drugs by consulting 3 major drug‐gene interaction databases (see Section 2 ). Manoalide (CHEMBL463914) emerged as the only compound reported to interact with DHX36 as part of its mechanism of action.

3.5 Tissue and Cell Type Prioritization Tissue and cell‐type enrichment analyzes highlighted blood vessels and blood‐derived cell types as nominally significant ( p < 0.05), with several immune‐related components such as granulocytes and lymphocytes emerging across methods (Table S12 ). To further refine these findings, we performed a targeted cell type analysis using single‐cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‐seq) data from blood and bone marrow, which identified dendritic cells as the most significantly enriched ( p < 0.05), suggesting a potential role in genetic susceptibility to FD. Finally, guided by the TWAS results implicating GI‐related tissues, we conducted a parallel scRNA‐seq‐based cell type analysis in GI tissues. This revealed enrichment ( p < 0.05) in enteroendocrine, vein/arterial endothelial cells, and dendritic cells, which are critical for gut barrier function and immune signaling.

FD — GP Genetic Overlap Given the widely reported similarity between FD and GP in clinical practice, including shared pathophysiological mechanisms, often indistinguishable symptoms, and even misdiagnosis [ 31 , 32 , 35 ], we decided to investigate whether these two conditions shared a common genetic liability. We therefore performed a GP GWAS meta‐analysis using a previously published pilot‐scale GWAS and a publicly available GWAS from the MVP cohort (see Section 2 ), thus including 3393 GP cases and 504,654 controls. We estimated the SNP‐based GP heritability on the liability scale to be between 8.3% and 19.5% ( p = 3.76 × 10 −10 ), depending on different estimations of population prevalence [ 31 , 32 ]. GP showed a significant but modest genetic correlation with FD ( r g = 0.33 ± 0.12, p = 5.30 × 10 −3 ), clearly below the estimates observed for IBS and GERD.

The pilot‐scale GP GWAS reported the strongest association signal at the HLA Class II region, tagged by the lead SNP rs9273363 and mapping the HLA‐DQB1 gene [ 30 ]. The same genetic signal was found at genome‐wide significant ( p = 3.92 × 10 −9 ) in the GP GWAS from the MVP cohort, which included a significant increase in the number of GP cases and total sample size. In concordance, this signal appeared as the sole genome‐wide significant association in the GP GWAS meta‐analysis (rs9273363 p = 2.95 × 10 −14 ; Figure 5 ).

4 Discussion In this study, we leveraged data from over 1 million individuals, including 29,584 FD cases, representing the largest and most comprehensive genetic investigation of FD to date. Despite this, we identified only one genome‐wide significant locus, indicating that the genetic contribution to FD is likely weak. Indeed, SNP‐based heritability of FD on the liability scale was estimated at around 3.6%, in concordance with previous estimates [ 9 ], and notably lower than other GI disorders such as IBS, GERD, or diverticular disease [ 36 , 37 ]. Furthermore, local heritability analyzes confirmed FD as a highly polygenic trait, adding to its genetic complexity. FD is therefore likely influenced by many contributing causal variants with relatively small effects and no single variant explaining a big proportion of the risk [ 38 ].

At a global level, genome‐wide genetic correlation analysis corroborated previously established genetic relationships with digestive and psychiatric conditions [ 9 ], and expanded its relationships with disorders of the musculoskeletal domain and other inflammatory‐driven disorders, as previously reported in epidemiological studies [ 39 ]. These analyzes also revealed that FD and GP, two disorders that have been proposed as part of a single disease spectrum from a clinical perspective [ 32 ], are genetically correlated yet represent distinct entities with different underlying genetic liabilities.

Further, MR analyzes revealed bidirectional causative effects of FD with IBS, GERD, and constipation, which remain inconclusive as to the real causative direction but evidence a common genetic etiology shaping these GI disorders. Conversely, we found strong evidence that anxiety and depression increase the genetic liability of FD, providing novel insight beyond epidemiological and observational studies consistently reporting significant associations between these traits [ 2 , 40 , 41 ]. Combined, these results reflect an overall influence of the brain‐gut axis in the pathophysiology of FD, albeit specific aetiological pathways remain elusive, as opposed to other DGBI, such as IBS [ 42 ]. Future studies should further elucidate the specific contributions of these closely related psychiatric traits which may help identify novel therapeutic strategies to improve the overall symptom burden in FD patients.

Alternatively, our bivariate analyzes revealed a higher genetic overlap at specific loci between FD and GI disorders, especially GERD, than with psychiatric traits. The high genetic overlap may, thus, help us understand FD biology through the identification of shared pathways and explain the overlapping symptomatology and frequent coexistence between GERD and FD [ 43 , 44 ]. The convergence of the high local genetic correlation in the HLA region with the genome‐wide significant signals existing in this complex region for other GI disorders may point toward an immune‐driven mechanism behind their pathophysiology [ 45 ]. The genome‐wide significant signal identified in the FD GWAS meta‐analysis was mapped to HLA Class II genes, which are of paramount importance for antigen presentation to CD4+ helper T cells and, therefore, adaptive immune responses to infections [ 46 ]. Of particular importance, the sole genome‐wide significant signal in the GP GWAS meta‐analysis mapped to the same HLA gene ( HLA‐DQB1 ), suggesting a possible common immunogenetic factor predisposing to upper gastrointestinal disorders. In this regard, the first GWAS of idiopathic achalasia, a gastrointestinal motility disorder affecting esophageal function, also identified its strongest genetic association within HLA‐DQB1 , further supporting the involvement of HLA Class II‐mediated immune mechanisms across disorders of the upper gastrointestinal tract [ 47 ]. Indeed, an immune hypothesis behind GERD, IBS, GP, and FD has been previously proposed, suggesting low‐grade inflammation, immune cell dysregulation, and barrier dysfunction may contribute to symptom generation [ 32 , 48 , 49 ]. Furthermore, there is increasing evidence pointing toward dysregulation of helper T cells as a key pathophysiological mechanism driving microinflammation in FD [ 50 , 51 ]. Finally, the stronger association observed in FinnGen suggests that this immunogenetic factor may contribute to FD susceptibility to a greater extent in individuals of Finnish ancestry than in other European populations. Although the consistent direction of effect across cohorts supports the overall association, confirmation in larger independent cohorts will be required to determine the magnitude and generalizability of this population‐related difference.

The integrative approach followed in the current study allowed convergence on a plausible candidate gene, DHX36 , supported by statistical association, tissue‐specific expression, and causal inference enhancing the biological interpretability of our findings. The genetic signals from the corresponding genomic risk locus may reflect a mechanism involving dysregulation of the DHX36 gene expression in several tissues across the GI tract. In particular, higher FD risk was linked to a reduced transcriptional activity of DHX36 in the esophagus, stomach, small intestine, and colon, potentially mediated by regulatory variants affecting transcription factor binding and local chromatin activity. This gene encodes a member of the DExD/H‐box helicase family, responsible for the recognition of viral nucleic acids as part of the innate immune system response against viral infections [ 52 ]. Recent evidence shows that loss of DHX36 leads to an increased production and secretion of proinflammatory cytokines [ 53 ]. The encoded protein functions primarily in myeloid and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, activating Type I interferon and inflammatory cytokines production. Our tissue and cell type prioritization analysis revealed enrichment of dendritic cells not only in the blood and bone marrow but also in intestinal tissues, suggesting a potentially relevant role in FD pathophysiology. Interestingly, DHX15 , another member of the DExD/H‐box helicase family, has been implicated in intestinal inflammation triggered by viral infections [ 54 ]. Taken together, the genetic evidence from our study alongside prior functional studies on DHX36 and related helicases supports the hypothesis that altered DHX36 activity may trigger low‐grade intestinal inflammation, thereby contributing to FD pathophysiology [ 5 , 48 ]. Thus, the strongest genetic signals identified in the present study point toward immune activation that leads to dysregulated cytokine production and subsequent mast cell and eosinophil recruitment, a recognized hallmark of FD [ 5 , 49 , 51 ]. Finally, to investigate the therapeutic relevance of DHX36 , we screened three major drug databases and identified Manoalide as a compound reported to interact with this gene, albeit not selectively. Manoalide is a potent analgesic and anti‐inflammatory, due to the inhibition of phospholipase A2 ( PLA2 ) [ 55 ]. By blocking calcium channels, manoalide has also been shown to prevent mast cell‐mediated inflammatory responses [ 56 ], a mechanism of particular relevance for FD. Further, preliminary evidence shows that manoalide inhibits the ATPase activity of human DHX36 potentially by targeting a conserved helicase domain [ 57 ], suggesting a possible functional interaction. Overall, the evidence linking DHX36 to FD provides strong rationale for testing related mechanisms and pathways in follow‐up genetic and experimental studies.

Our study has intrinsic limitations that need to be acknowledged. First, phenotype definition was based on ICD10/Phecodes, which are efficient at scale but may introduce more variability across centres than gold‐standard Rome criteria. Second, participants were exclusively of European ancestry, which limits the portability of the genetic effects estimates to other ancestries.

Notwithstanding these constraints, this study provides better insights into the complex polygenic architecture of FD, highlighting immune‐mediated mechanisms and individual candidate genes that merit further investigation in independent, deeply phenotyped FD cohorts based on current Rome criteria. Integrating genetic evidence with complementary biological samples and molecular data may further clarify the mechanisms implicated by DHX36 and their relevance to FD pathophysiology. Author information: (1)1 FMH Gastroenterologie, Ärztehaus Fluntern, Zürich. Functional gastrointestinal complaints are very common in daily clinic practice. Functional gastrointestinal disorders are characterized in disturbances of motility patterns and/or of visceral hypersensitivity. The main functional gastrointestinal disorders are functional dyspepsia and irritable bowel syndrome. There is no causative therapy, but we have many medication and also non-medication therapeutic options which all can be tried on an indivual basis.
